# LiDAR Developer Guide

> Developer guide for SICK LRS4000, multiScan100, multiScan200, and picoScan100 LiDAR sensors, with setup, configuration, data streaming, and integration.

Source: https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/

# LiDAR Developer Guide

Integrate SICK LRS4000, multiScan100, multiScan200, and picoScan100 LiDAR sensors into your application. Connect, configure through REST or CoLa, stream measurement data, and use the data in your application. Pick your device, or jump to a topic.

# Getting Started with SICK LiDAR Sensors

> Connect a SICK LiDAR sensor, open its web interface at the default IP 192.168.0.1, and check the first measurement data in Wireshark.

Source: https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/getting-started/

# Getting Started

Compatible with: LRS4000 multiScan100 multiScan200 picoScan100

Use this page once for every new sensor. It takes you from a powered sensor to
the web interface and to the first measurement data on your computer.

## Connect the Sensor

Connect the sensor to the computer with Ethernet, either with a cable between them or through a network switch. The device must be powered, and at least one LED must be green. For the connector layout and pin assignment, see the electrical connection page for [LRS4000](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/LRS4000/electrical-connection/), [multiScan100](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/multiScan100/electrical-connection/), [multiScan200](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/multiScan200/electrical-connection/), or [picoScan100](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/picoScan100/electrical-connection/).

Give the computer's Ethernet adapter a static address in the sensor subnet. No gateway is needed to communicate within this subnet.

<div class="centered-table" markdown>

<p class="table-caption" markdown>**Connect the Sensor:** device, IP address, and subnet mask.</p>

| Device   | IP address      | Subnet mask     |
| -------- | --------------- | --------------- |
| Sensor   | `192.168.0.1`   | `255.255.255.0` |
| Computer | `192.168.0.100` | `255.255.255.0` |

</div>

The factory sensor address is `192.168.0.1` for LRS4000, multiScan100,
multiScan200, and picoScan100. Check the device label or the saved project
documentation if the sensor does not respond at that address.

=== "Windows"

    Open **Settings → Network & internet → Ethernet → IP assignment → Edit**, select **Manual**, enable IPv4, and enter the computer's values:

    ![Windows Ethernet IPv4 settings for a sensor connection](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/assets/picoScan100/img/windows-ip-settings.png){ width="344" }
    *Example Windows configuration for an Ethernet connection to the sensor.*

    Set the network profile of this adapter to **Private**. A Public profile blocks inbound UDP data, device discovery replies, and DDS discovery. In PowerShell, replace `18` with the interface index that `Get-NetConnectionProfile` reports for the sensor adapter:

    ```powershell
    Get-NetConnectionProfile
    Set-NetConnectionProfile -InterfaceIndex 18 -NetworkCategory Private
    ```

=== "Linux"

    Add the computer's address to the adapter connected to the sensor. Replace `eth0` with your interface name from `ip link`. The address is lost on reboot; use `nmcli` for a permanent setting.

    ```bash
    sudo ip addr add 192.168.0.100/24 dev eth0
    ```

## Open the Web Interface

Open `http://<sensor-ip>/` in Chrome, Edge, or Firefox. With factory settings, use <http://192.168.0.1/>.

![SOPASair Home page opened at 192.168.0.1](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/assets/getting-started/sopasair-home.png)
*SOPASair Home page opened at 192.168.0.1.*

If the page does not load, check the subnet settings above or [find the sensor on the network](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/shared-features/device-discovery/).

*picoScan100 example: Connect to the sensor in a web browser after configuring the computer's network adapter.*

## Log In

Reading values needs no login. Changing settings requires a login with an enabled [user level](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/shared-features/user-levels/). On all devices, only **Service** is enabled by default. In SOPASair, open the login dialog, select **Service**, and enter its password. Then enable only the levels required by the deployment. The default passwords are documented in the operating instructions of your device. Do not pass them on, and change them during commissioning.

*SOPASair login: select a user level and enter its password to access configuration settings.*

## Change the IP Address

To use the sensor in your own network, give it an address in that network:

1. In the web interface, log in and open **Configuration → Connection options**.
2. Set **Addressing mode** to **Static**, or to **DHCP** if a DHCP server assigns the address.
3. Enter the **IP address**, **Subnet mask**, and **Default gateway**. The IP address must be unique in the network.
4. Click **Apply**. The browser loses the connection to the sensor.
5. If the new address is in another subnet, change the computer's Ethernet adapter accordingly. Then open the web interface at the new address and click **Save permanently**.

![Ethernet settings in the web interface](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/assets/picoScan100/img/sopasair-configuration-ethernet-tile.png){ width="300" }
*Ethernet settings under **Configuration → Connection options**.*

*picoScan100 example: Change the device IP address through the web interface. For restrictions on device search, see the IP Address Assignment page.*

## Receive and Explore Measurement Data 

Use Compact for a first measurement-data check on all four devices:

1. In SOPASair, log in, open **Application > Data output**, and set the output
   for your device:

    === "LRS4000"

        Select **Compact** as the output format.

    === "multiScan100 / picoScan100"

        Select **Compact**, set the UDP destination to your computer's IP
        address (for example, `192.168.0.100`) and port `2115`, then enable
        **Start/stop data output**.

        ![SOPASair measurement data output set to Compact over UDP, port 2115, destination 192.168.0.100, with data output, RSSI, and properties enabled](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/assets/getting-started/compact-udp-output.png){ width="340" }
        *picoScan100 example: Compact UDP output to the development computer.*

    === "multiScan200"

        Enable **TCP Compact** measurement-data output.

    Apply the settings and use **Save permanently** to retain them after a restart.

2. Install [Wireshark](https://www.wireshark.org/download.html) with the
   [Compact dissector](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/data-streaming/compact-format/#install-the-dissector),
   then capture on the Ethernet interface connected to the sensor.
3. LRS4000 and multiScan200 send Compact over TCP. Connect a TCP client to the
   sensor's IP address on port `2115` and keep the connection open.
   Wireshark captures traffic but does not open the connection itself.
4. Enter `compact` in Wireshark's display-filter bar. Select a `COMPACT` packet
   and expand its decoded fields to inspect distances and scan metadata.
   If none appear, clear the filter and check the output settings and connection.

![Wireshark with the compact display filter and an expanded Compact measurement-data packet showing scan metadata](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/assets/getting-started/wireshark-compact-measurement-data.png)
*picoScan150 example: Compact packets and decoded scan metadata in Wireshark.*

Next: [REST Interface](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/configuration/rest-interface/) ·
[Compact Format](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/data-streaming/compact-format/) ·
[ROS Integration](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/integration-notes/ros-integration/)

# LiDAR Basics: Time-of-Flight, Echoes, and Scanning

> How LiDAR sensors measure distance with laser pulses, what remission and echoes mean, and how 2D scans and 3D point clouds are created.

Source: https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/lidar-basics/

# LiDAR Basics

Compatible with: LRS4000 multiScan100 multiScan200 picoScan100

LiDAR stands for light detection and ranging. A LiDAR sensor sends out laser
pulses and evaluates the light that comes back from objects. Every measurement
produces a distance and the direction the beam pointed in, so the sensor maps
its surroundings without touching anything.

The sensor supplies its own light. It therefore works in daylight, at night,
indoors, and in tunnels. This page explains the measuring principle and the
terms used throughout this guide. Short definitions are collected in the
[glossary](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/glossary/).

## Measuring Distance with Light

![Pulse time-of-flight measurement: an emitted pulse travels to a truck and returns to the sensor after the time t1](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/assets/lidar-basics/time-of-flight.png){ width="70%" }
*The sensor measures the time between the emitted pulse and the received pulse.*

A pulse leaves the sender, travels to the object, and part of it returns to the
receiver. The sensor measures the elapsed time. Light travels at a known speed
and covers the distance twice, so the distance is half the time-of-flight
multiplied by the speed of light.

The beam follows a straight line, so the sensor reports the shortest distance to
the first object in its path. Two pulse time-of-flight implementations are
relevant here:

<p class="table-caption" markdown>**Measuring Distance with Light:** process, how it works, and strength.</p>

| Process                     | How it works                                                           | Strength                                                  |
| --------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------- |
| Single-pulse time-of-flight | Determines a distance from the travel time of one pulse and its echo.  | Direct measurement with a short response time.            |
| HDDM+                       | Combines the returns from many pulses to calculate one distance value. | Reliable readings on dark objects and in poor visibility. |

Both implementations determine distance from the travel time of light. HDDM+
uses the additional measurements to make the result more robust.

## How Much Light Comes Back

![Diffuse reflection: a laser beam hits a rough surface and is scattered in many directions](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/assets/lidar-basics/reflection-diffuse.png){ width="70%" }
*A rough surface scatters the beam, so only a fraction of the light returns to the receiver.*

Most surfaces scatter light in many directions, and only a small part of it
reaches the receiver. The share of light that an object sends back is its
[remission factor](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/glossary/#remission-factor). It determines how far away that object can
still be measured.

<p class="table-caption" markdown>**How Much Light Comes Back:** surface and approximate remission.</p>

| Surface                  | Approximate remission |
| ------------------------ | --------------------- |
| Coal                     | 5 %                   |
| Matte black shoe leather | 10 %                  |
| White drywall            | 90 %                  |
| Reflective tape          | Several 1,000 %       |
| Retroreflector           | Up to 10,000 %        |

Scanning ranges are therefore always stated together with a remission factor,
for example 30 m at 10 % remission. A dark object is detected at a shorter
distance than a bright one, and retroreflectors return far more light than a
diffuse surface.

The beam needs a clear line of sight. A LiDAR sensor does not see around
corners and generally cannot measure through glass or film packaging. Such
surfaces create reflections of their own and disturb the measured value.

## One Beam, Several Echoes

![A LiDAR beam passing through fog and rain before reaching a solid object, with the strength of each return shown below](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/assets/lidar-basics/multi-echo.png){ width="70%" }
*Fog, rain, and the solid object each produce a different return signal.*

A laser pulse is not infinitely thin. When the beam hits a raindrop, a dust
cloud, or the edge of an object, part of the light is reflected early while the
rest travels on to the surface behind. Every reflection that reaches the
receiver is an echo, and the sensor can report more than one echo per beam.

Echoes are what make LiDAR usable outdoors, because reflections from rain,
snow, dust, and hail can be separated from the real target. The
[echo filter](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/data-streaming/filter-details/#echo-filter) selects which echoes
the sensor outputs, for example the first echo, the last echo, or all of them.

## One, Two, and Three Dimensions

<p class="table-caption" markdown>**One, Two, and Three Dimensions:** variant, what it measures, and typical sensor.</p>

| Variant | What it measures                                | Typical sensor                                    |
| ------- | ----------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- |
| 1D      | Distance along a single fixed beam.             | Distance sensor aimed at a target or a reflector. |
| 2D      | Distance and angle within one plane.            | 2D LiDAR sensor, also called a laser scanner.     |
| 3D      | Distance, horizontal angle, and vertical angle. | Multi-layer sensor, or a 2D sensor that is moved. |

The horizontal angle of a beam is called the azimuth and the vertical angle the
elevation.

## How a 2D Sensor Scans a Plane

![Cutaway view of a 2D LiDAR sensor deflecting its beam with a rotating mirror toward an object](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/assets/lidar-basics/2d-scanning-principle.png){ width="70%" }
*A rotating mirror sweeps the beam of one sender and receiver across a whole plane.*

A 2D sensor deflects its beam with a rotating mirror, so a single sender and
receiver cover an entire plane. The sensor fires its pulses in step with the
mirror rotation. This links three values: the pulse rate of the laser, the
rotation speed of the motor, and the angular resolution.

Angular resolution is the angle between two neighboring measured points.

![Comparison of a scan with coarse angular resolution and a scan with fine angular resolution](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/assets/lidar-basics/angular-resolution.png){ width="70%" }
*A fine angular resolution places the measured points closer together.*

A fine angular resolution puts the measured points close together and covers the
scan plane without gaps, so even small objects are detected. A coarse angular
resolution produces fewer points per scan. The beam also widens with distance,
so the points move further apart the further away the object is. A scan that
covers an area without gaps nearby can leave gaps at long range.

One full scan of the plane is called a frame. The sensors in this guide output
each frame in segments, and filters can reduce the data before it is sent. See
[Data Streaming](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/data-streaming/) and
[Filter Details](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/data-streaming/filter-details/).

## From Scan Planes to Point Clouds

![3D LiDAR sensor scanning a stack of pallets with four stacked scan planes](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/assets/lidar-basics/multi-layer-planes.png){ width="70%" }
*A multi-layer sensor scans several planes at once, each tilted by a fixed angle.*

A 3D sensor adds the vertical angle. Multi-layer sensors contain several sender
and receiver modules aimed at different vertical angles, so one rotation
produces several scan planes, called layers, at the same time. Distance,
azimuth, and elevation together describe every measured point as an XYZ
coordinate. A set of such points is a point cloud.

![A SICK multiScan sensor using multiple scan planes to measure horizontal and vertical surfaces](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/assets/lidar-basics/multiscan-3d-coverage.png){ width="70%" }
*Multiple scan planes provide the spatial coverage needed to build a 3D view.*

A 2D sensor can also produce 3D data when it is moved, for example on a rotating
axis, a linear axis, or a vehicle. The scans carry time stamps, and the known
movement supplies the missing third coordinate. See
[3D With 2D LiDARs](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/integration-notes/3d-with-2d-lidars/).

# SICK Virtual Sensor Lab: Try LiDAR Sensors in the Browser

> Use the SICK Virtual Sensor Lab to run virtual LRS4000, multiScan100, multiScan200, and picoScan100 web interfaces in the browser.

Source: https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/simulation/virtual-sensor-lab/

# Virtual Sensor Lab

Compatible with: LRS4000 multiScan100 multiScan200 picoScan100

The cloud-based SICK Virtual Sensor Lab runs a live virtual sensor in your browser, so you can explore its web UI without hardware.

Open it at [devices.cloud.sick.com](https://devices.cloud.sick.com/).

- Explore every menu of the web UI and change settings, for example the data output or field-evaluation zones.
- Prepare a configuration offline, export it, and import it into a real device later. Configuration files from real devices can also be loaded and viewed.
- It does not replace commissioning or a function test on the real device. `.sopas` files cannot be imported or exported.

![SICK Virtual Sensor Lab LiDAR product selection](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/assets/simulation/virtual-sensor-lab-lidar-products.png)
*SICK Virtual Sensor Lab product selection interface.*

# LiDAR Simulation Overview

> Explore SICK LiDAR web interfaces in the Virtual Sensor Lab or simulate sensor measurements in NVIDIA Isaac Sim before hardware is available.

Source: https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/simulation/

# Simulation

Choose a virtual web interface to explore device configuration, or a robotics
simulator to test sensor models in a scene.

* [Virtual Sensor Lab](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/simulation/virtual-sensor-lab/): run virtual sensor web interfaces in your browser.
* [NVIDIA Isaac Sim](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/simulation/nvidia-isaac-sim/): use SICK LiDAR models in simulated environments.

# SICK LiDAR Models in NVIDIA Isaac Sim

> Simulate SICK LRS4000, multiScan100, and picoScan100 LiDAR models in NVIDIA Isaac Sim before hardware is available. multiScan200 is coming soon.

Source: https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/simulation/nvidia-isaac-sim/

# NVIDIA Isaac Sim

Compatible with: LRS4000 multiScan100 picoScan100

<div class="tool-intro" markdown>

![NVIDIA](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/assets/simulation/nvidia-logo.png)
NVIDIA Isaac Sim provides simulation environments for robotics, industrial automation, and autonomous systems. SICK LiDAR models let you test applications and algorithms before physical hardware is available.

</div>

SICK models are available for picoScan150, picoScan120, multiScan136, multiScan165, and LRS4581R. multiScan200 models are coming soon. Find them on the applicable SICK product page under **Downloads > Software** or in NVIDIA Omniverse's sensor library. Configure the mounting position, orientation, field of view, scan frequency, detection range, and environment to match the deployment.

Search for the product family on sick.com:

- [LRS4000](https://www.sick.com/de/en/search?text=LRS4000)

# SOPASair: The Built-In LiDAR Web Interface

> SOPASair is the built-in web interface for SICK LRS4000, multiScan100, multiScan200, and picoScan100 sensors.

Source: https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/visualization/sopasair/

# SOPASair

Compatible with: LRS4000 multiScan100 multiScan200 picoScan100

SOPASair is the sensor's built-in web UI, served directly from the device at `http://192.168.0.1/` with factory settings. There is nothing to install: point a browser at the sensor. Use it to:

- configure the settings available on the selected device,
- draw or teach in field-evaluation zones where the device supports those functions,
- update firmware through the web UI where supported, or use the documented [REST sequence](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/shared-features/firmware-update/),
- create a diagnostic file if the device provides that option.

Screen-by-screen walkthroughs are available for the [LRS4000](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/LRS4000/graphical-user-interface/), [multiScan100](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/multiScan100/graphical-user-interface/), [multiScan200](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/multiScan200/graphical-user-interface/), and [picoScan100](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/picoScan100/graphical-user-interface/). Available menus and functions vary by product family, variant, and firmware. For standard IP address settings, see [Getting Started](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/getting-started/).

For measurement recordings, see the [SOPASair Data recorder](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/recording/sopasair/) if that function is available on your device.

![SOPASair user interface overview](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/assets/picoScan100/img/sopasair-home.png)
*Live capture from a picoScan100's SOPASair web interface.*

# LiDAR Visualization: SOPASair, SOPAS ET, rviz2, and More

> Choose SICK LiDAR software for live sensor setup, device commissioning, ROS topic checks, or offline point-cloud viewing.

Source: https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/visualization/

# Choose a Visualization Tool

Choose a tool based on whether you need to configure a live sensor, manage
devices and firmware, locate a device, or inspect point-cloud files.

* [SOPASair](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/visualization/sopasair/): configure and commission a connected sensor in its browser-based interface, including interactive workflows such as field teach-in and firmware update. Start here.
* [ROS 2 rviz](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/visualization/rviz2/): view live ROS 2 topics and point clouds to check data flow, frame alignment, and scan coverage; requires a running ROS 2 setup.
* [CloudCompare](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/visualization/cloudcompare/): inspect and process saved 3D point clouds, including compatible PCD files; for offline work, not live sensor configuration.
* [Sentio Creator](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/visualization/sentio-creator/): discover and commission SICK devices and find matching firmware packages; requires installing the SICK software.
* [SOPAS ET](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/visualization/sopas-et/): use the legacy engineering tool across all device families for network discovery and CoLa commands; use SOPASair for supported device setup.

# View LiDAR Point Clouds (PCD) in CloudCompare

> Open and inspect .pcd point clouds from 3D scan recording or the sick_perception_sdk in the free CloudCompare viewer.

Source: https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/visualization/cloudcompare/

# CloudCompare

Compatible with: LRS4000 multiScan100 multiScan200 picoScan100

<div class="tool-intro" markdown>

![CloudCompare](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/assets/visualization/cloudcompare-logo.svg)
CloudCompare is a free, open-source 3D point-cloud viewer and processing tool. You can use it to visualize `.pcd` files produced by 3D scan recording or by the [sick_perception_sdk](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/recording/sick-perception-sdk/), without writing any viewer code yourself.

</div>

![CloudCompare 2.13.2 displaying a green LiDAR point cloud with the About CloudCompare dialog open](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/assets/visualization/cloudcompare.png)
*LiDAR point cloud displayed in CloudCompare 2.13.2.*

1. Open the `.pcd` file with **File → Open**.
2. If the file contains intensity, select the cloud and set **Colors** to **Scalar field** with intensity as the active field in the **Properties** panel.
3. Use the **Point picking** tool to measure the distance between two points.

# ROS 2 rviz: Visualize LiDAR Data

> Use rviz2 to visualize SICK LiDAR point clouds and topics in ROS 2 before any custom application code is written.

Source: https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/visualization/rviz2/

# ROS 2 rviz

Compatible with: LRS4000 multiScan100 multiScan200 picoScan100

<div class="tool-intro" markdown>

![ROS 2](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/assets/integration-notes/ros2-logo.png)
Use `rviz2` to inspect SICK LiDAR point clouds, laser scans, and coordinate
frames from native ROS 2 or `sick_scan_xd`.

</div>

1. Configure the sensor for ROS 2 output as described in [ROS Integration](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/integration-notes/ros-integration/).
2. Start the ROS 2 middleware and sensor publisher. For native ROS 2, use
   Cyclone DDS; for `sick_scan_xd`, start the driver on the host.
3. Confirm that ROS 2 can see the sensor topics:

   ```bash
   ros2 topic list
   ```

   For native ROS 2, `/cloud/all_points` is the combined point cloud. A
   `sick_scan_xd` launch can use different topic names; select the
   `sensor_msgs/msg/PointCloud2` or `sensor_msgs/msg/LaserScan` topic shown by
   `ros2 topic list`.
4. Launch `rviz2` in the same sourced ROS 2 environment:

   ```bash
   rviz2
   ```

5. In the left panel, add a display such as:
   - `PointCloud2` for a dense 3D point cloud,
   - `LaserScan` for 2D planar output,
   - `TF` to verify coordinate frames,
   - `Axes` to confirm sensor orientation.
6. Select the published topic, set the fixed frame, and check the sensor data
   against the expected field of view.

Set **Reliability Policy** to match the publisher when rviz2 reports an
incompatible QoS profile. Check that data arrives on the topic:

```bash
ros2 topic info --verbose /cloud/all_points
ros2 topic echo --once /cloud/all_points
```

Replace the topic for a `sick_scan_xd` launch. If data arrives but rviz2 shows a
**No transform** error, set **Fixed Frame** to the message's
`header.frame_id`, or publish the required static transform.

# LiDAR On-Device Applications Overview

> Explore SICK LiDAR field evaluation, object detection, perpendicular-distance measurement, contamination indication, and 3D scan recording.

Source: https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/on-device-applications/

# On-Device Applications

Use sensor-side processing to obtain application results without processing
every scan point on a host. Check each page for supported devices and limits.

* [Field Evaluation](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/on-device-applications/field-evaluation/): configure evaluation fields and read their results.
* [Object Evaluation](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/on-device-applications/object-evaluation/): use multiScan100 object properties to make decisions based on object criteria.
* [Perpendicular Distance Measurement](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/on-device-applications/perpendicular-distance-measurement/): measure distance relative to a reference plane.
* [Contamination Indication](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/on-device-applications/contamination-indication/): monitor dirt on the optics cover.
* [3D Scan Recording](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/on-device-applications/3d-scan-recording/): record a 3D point cloud with a rotating 2D sensor.

# LiDAR Field Evaluation: Polygons, Teach-In, and REST API

> Configure on-device field evaluation on LRS4000, multiScan100, multiScan200, and picoScan100: evaluation groups, polygons via GUI, REST, or CoLa, and teach-in.

Source: https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/on-device-applications/field-evaluation/

# Field Evaluation

Compatible with: LRS4000 multiScan100 multiScan200 picoScan100

The sensor evaluates detection zones on the device. Field evaluation checks whether scan points enter a configured polygon and reports whether the field is free or infringed. The result can drive a digital output and can be read through REST, CoLa, or WebSocket events. In SOPASair, field evaluation is the **Object Detection** application; both names mean the same function.

<p class="table-caption" markdown>**Field Evaluation:** term and meaning.</p>

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Evaluation | One field (polygon) with its detection parameters, stored in an evaluation slot |
| Evaluation slot | Numbered storage place for one evaluation, for example `Eval001` |
| Group | One or more evaluations that are activated together |
| Activation type | When a group is evaluated: always, by digital inputs, or by telegram |
| Result | Per evaluation: free or infringed; per group: active, inactive, or not configured |

*picoScan100: How to draw fields and detect objects?*

## Configure in the Web GUI

Open the **Object Detection** application in SOPASair to create and edit polygon points directly. This is the quickest method for commissioning and manual adjustments. The field editor also supports teach-in.

![Field evaluation teach-in tile](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/assets/picoScan100/img/sopasair-application-field-evaluation-teach-in-tile.png)
*Field evaluation teach-in tile in SOPASair.*

For bulk coordinate changes, open the Field settings dialog and select JSON in its footer toolbar. The editor switches from the coordinate table to a JSON text field. Paste the prepared polygon to replace all points at once:

```json
{
  "points": [
    { "x": -5, "y": 531 },
    { "x": 837, "y": 565 },
    { "x": 907, "y": -637 },
    { "x": 12, "y": -590 }
  ]
}
```

### Copy to Other Devices

Use the top-right SOPASair menu to download the complete configuration from a commissioned sensor. It includes field geometries and can be imported into another compatible device, making it suitable for repeatable commissioning and replacement devices. Keep a versioned, validated backup for each deployed configuration.

## Teach In

Teach-in captures the current environment and uses the measured contour as a field for object detection. Use it during commissioning when the surrounding geometry should define the detection field instead of drawing a polygon manually.

Open the **Object Detection** application in SOPASair and select **Teach-in** in the field configuration. Set the distances in front of and behind the object, choose the minimum teach-in time, and click **Start**. Stop the teach-in when the environment has been captured, then save the field evaluation configuration.

*Teach-in configuration in SOPASair.*

The configured distances take effect during the next teach-in. Keep the intended environment stable while the contour is captured.

Teach-in uses the same evaluation group and output mechanism as a manually configured field. After the contour has been captured, monitor the evaluation result through the configured output, REST, CoLa, or WebSocket events.

## Minimum Object Size

The farther an object is, the wider apart the beams are, so small objects can fall between them.
Select a device family, scan configuration, target, and object size to estimate up to which range the object is still detected.
Device presets fill in the model-specific values from the operating instructions. Select **Custom Values** to adjust angular resolution, beam divergence, minimum spot size, and scanning range.

## Activate and Monitor a Group

<p class="table-caption" markdown>**Activate and Monitor a Group:** REST resource and purpose.</p>

| REST resource | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `ActivateEvaluationGroup` | Activates or deactivates a `TELEGRAM`-controlled group |
| `FieldEvaluationGroupState` | Group state: not configured, active, or inactive |
| `FieldEvaluationResult` | Current result: `FREE`, `INFRINGED`, or a transitional state; also available as a [WebSocket event](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/data-streaming/websocket-events/) |

A typical application creates the groups once, persists the configuration, and at runtime reads the group state and result, updates contours when necessary, and switches telegram-controlled groups.

For full payloads, see the [LRS4000](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/LRS4000/api-rest-openapi/), [multiScan100](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/multiScan100/api-rest-openapi/), [multiScan200](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/multiScan200/api-rest-openapi/), and [picoScan100](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/picoScan100/api-rest-openapi/) REST API references and the CoLa telegram listings for [LRS4000](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/LRS4000/api-cola-telegrams/), [multiScan100](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/multiScan100/api-cola-telegrams/), [multiScan200](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/multiScan200/api-cola-telegrams/), and [picoScan100](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/picoScan100/api-cola-telegrams/).

Activation types (`Activation.Type` of a group). `ActivateEvaluationGroup` only switches `TELEGRAM` groups:

<p class="table-caption" markdown>**Activate and Monitor a Group:** value, type, and behavior.</p>

| Value | Type | Behavior |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `0` | Deactivated | The group is never evaluated. |
| `1` | Always | The group is active as soon as it is stored. `ActivateEvaluationGroup` returns `false` for it and cannot switch it off. |
| `2` | Inputs | Digital inputs activate the group. |
| `3` | Telegram | The group starts in the state set by `InitialActivationStateTelegram` and is switched with `ActivateEvaluationGroup`. |

`FieldEvaluationGroupState` returns one value per group: `0` not configured, `1` active, `2` inactive. `FieldEvaluationResult` returns one state per evaluation: `0` not configured, `1` inactive, `2` free, `3` detecting infringed, `4` infringed, `5` detecting free.

## Configure over the API

On all devices, create the evaluations in SOPASair or restore them from a [configuration file](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/configuration/configuration-backup-and-restore/); REST and CoLa can then change them. On the picoScan100, REST and CoLa can also build complete evaluations from scratch. The following workflow applies to picoScan150 with firmware V2.3.3. Some of these variables, such as `Eval001`–`Eval048` and `EvaluationGroupMapping`, are not listed in the published OpenAPI file, but can be read and written as REST variables (`GET` / `POST /api/<Variable>`).

<p class="table-caption" markdown>**Configure over the API:** variable or method, purpose, and devices.</p>

| Variable or method | Purpose | Devices |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Eval001`–`Eval048` | Detection parameters of one evaluation slot: mode, minimum object size, timing, and the referenced volume (`VolumeList`) | picoScan100 |
| `SetFieldEvaluationContour` / `GetFieldEvaluationContour` | Writes or reads the polygon of an evaluation | LRS4000, multiScan100, multiScan200, picoScan100 |
| `SetFieldEvaluationConfiguration` / `GetFieldEvaluationConfiguration` | Writes or reads evaluation parameters | multiScan200 |
| `EvaluationGroupMapping` | Groups evaluations and sets the activation type of each group | picoScan100 |
| `EvaluationGroupType` | Selects field evaluation or perpendicular-distance mode | LRS4000, picoScan100 |
| `PortConfiguration` | Assigns an evaluation result to a digital output | LRS4000, multiScan100, multiScan200, picoScan100 |
| `WriteEeprom` (REST) / `mEEwriteall` (CoLa) | Stores the configuration permanently | LRS4000, multiScan100, multiScan200, picoScan100 |

To create an evaluation on the picoScan100, log in as **Authorized client** or **Service** and write the variables in this order:

1. Write `EvalNNN` with the detection mode, the minimum object size, and `VolumeList = [NNN]`.
2. Write the polygon with `SetFieldEvaluationContour`. It returns error `1` (invalid evaluation) if `VolumeList` of the slot is empty, so write the slot first.
3. Write `EvaluationGroupMapping`. The whole array is replaced on every write: read the current mapping first and include every group you want to keep.
4. Optional: write `PortConfiguration` to switch a digital output when the evaluation is infringed. Outputs refer to evaluations (sources `EG01`–`EG48`), not to groups, and the whole port array must be written.
5. Call `WriteEeprom`. The device re-initializes; wait about 1 s before reading the state.
6. For a `TELEGRAM` group, switch it on with `ActivateEvaluationGroup`.

To delete an evaluation, remove its group from `EvaluationGroupMapping`, clear `VolumeList` and the name of the slot, and call `WriteEeprom`. The group state returns to not configured.

The coordinates are in millimeters in the sensor coordinate system: `x` points forward (depth) and `y` to the side.

**Detection modes** (`EvaluationParamsCommon.Mode` of the evaluation slot):

<p class="table-caption" markdown>**Configure over the API:** value, mode, and the field is infringed when.</p>

| Value | Mode | The field is infringed when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `0` | Blanking | An object at least as large as the minimum object size is inside the field. This is the most common mode. |
| `1` | Reflector only | A highly reflective object such as a retroreflector is inside the field. |
| `2` | Contour | The scan deviates from the taught-in contour by more than the tolerance. Requires a valid [teach-in](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/on-device-applications/field-evaluation/#teach-in-over-the-api). |

### Change a Polygon

The REST API exposes `SetFieldEvaluationContour` to update a polygon. The evaluation must already exist. Use `GetFieldEvaluationContour` to confirm the stored geometry and persist the change with `WriteEeprom`. See the [REST client example](https://github.com/SICKAG/sick_scan_rest_client/blob/public/examples/sick_scan_rest_client_object_detection_example.py).

CoLa provides the same `SetFieldEvaluationContour` function through its telegram interface. Use it when the integration already uses CoLa, such as a PLC or legacy client; see [CoLa](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/configuration/cola-interface/).

The `sick_perception_sdk` uses the REST interface and provides an application-level option for changing contours. See the [object-detection example](https://github.com/SICKAG/sick_perception_sdk/blob/main/examples/shared/object_detection.cpp).

## Teach in over the API

A teach-in evaluation is an evaluation slot with mode `2` (contour). The polygon written with `SetFieldEvaluationContour` is not the detection field: it is the region of interest in which teach-in learns the reference contour. `GetFieldEvaluationContour` therefore returns this region, not the learned contour.

Teach-in is global; it is not bound to an evaluation slot. Set the parameters, then start and stop the teach-in:

<p class="table-caption" markdown>**Teach in over the API:** variable or method and purpose.</p>

| Variable or method | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `TeachInToleranceFront` / `TeachInToleranceBack` | Tolerance in front of and behind the taught contour, in mm (default 250) |
| `TeachInMinimumTimeMs` | Minimum teach-in time, 100 to 60000 ms (default 250) |
| `TeachInActivationInput` | Digital input that starts the teach-in; `0` = software only |
| `StartTeachIn` / `StopTeachIn` | Starts and stops the teach-in |
| `TeachInActive` | `1` while the teach-in runs |
| `TeachInContourValid` | `1` after a teach-in produced a valid contour |

Keep the scene stable for at least the minimum teach-in time, stop the teach-in, check `TeachInContourValid`, and call `WriteEeprom`. To change the field later, repeat the teach-in, for example with a larger tolerance; the region of interest stays the same.

## Distance-Dependent

The **Distance-dependent** parameter determines whether two detected objects are evaluated separately or merged into one object based on their axial separation. It works with the configured **Blanking** width to avoid triggering a field evaluation when separate small objects would otherwise appear as one large object.

*picoScan100: 2D Object Detection Parameter Distance-dependent.*

The video uses two objects: a foreground object approximately 60 mm wide, a background object approximately 250 mm wide, and about 450 mm of axial separation. The standard blanking width is 300 mm.

<p class="table-caption" markdown>**Example:** configuration, result, and explanation.</p>

| Configuration | Result | Explanation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Distance-dependent off | Field infringed | Both objects merge into one contiguous object wider than 300 mm. |
| Distance-dependent on; threshold 300 mm | Field not infringed | The objects are at least 300 mm apart and are evaluated separately; neither is wider than 300 mm. |
| Distance-dependent on; threshold 500 mm | Field infringed | The objects are less than 500 mm apart, so they merge and exceed the blanking width. |

Set the separation threshold to the distance at which nearby objects should be merged for your application.

## Ground Filter (multiScan100)

The ground filter uses upper and lower ground thresholds to reduce false
field-evaluation triggers caused by the ground. When configured correctly, it
retains small objects such as forklift tines and can be used indoors and
outdoors. The filter also affects perpendicular-distance evaluations. See
[Ground Filter](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/data-streaming/filter-details/#ground-filter) for
availability and API settings.

*multiScan1xx: Ground-filter behavior in a field application.*

# LiDAR Object Evaluation with multiScan100

> Configure multiScan100 object evaluation using tracked object properties, spatial regions, motion criteria, and REST result states.

Source: https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/on-device-applications/object-evaluation/

# Object Evaluation

Compatible with: multiScan100

**Object Evaluation** combines 3D object tracking with configurable criteria.
The tracker estimates each object's track ID, horizontal and vertical size,
speed, direction of movement, and age. An evaluation checks those properties
within a configured region and reports whether its criteria are met. This lets
an application respond to relevant movement without processing every scan
point on a host.

*multiScan100 Object Evaluation overview: tracked objects are evaluated against configured regions and criteria.*

![SOPASair Object Evaluation view with tracked objects and their properties](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/assets/multiScan100/img/firmware-250-object-evaluation-light.png)
*The multiScan100 3D view displays tracked-object IDs, dimensions, speed, direction of movement, and age alongside the configured evaluation regions.*

Object Evaluation is available from multiScan100 firmware 2.5.0 and requires
the **3D Object Detection Advanced** package. Check the device variant,
firmware, and installed license before commissioning. See the
[firmware 2.5.0 release notes](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/multiScan100/release-notes/#firmware-250)
and [multiScan100 license list](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/multiScan100/licenses/).

Object Evaluation filters tracked objects by measurable properties; it does
not return semantic object-class labels. Validate any application decision
against the real objects and operating conditions.

## How an Evaluation Works

Object tracking estimates object properties over successive scans. An
evaluation then applies its spatial region and criteria to those tracks. The
result is a state for each configured evaluation, not a class label for each
object.

<p class="table-caption" markdown>**Object Evaluation criteria:** region and track properties used to determine whether an evaluation is infringed.</p>

| Criterion | How it affects the evaluation |
| --- | --- |
| Region of interest | A polygon in the scan plane, with lower and upper Z limits, defines where objects are evaluated. |
| Object size | Minimum horizontal and vertical sizes can be set. An optional maximum-size filter rejects objects that exceed the configured maximum dimensions. |
| Motion state | `ALL` accepts moving and stationary tracks; `MOVING` or `STATIONARY` restricts the evaluation to that motion state. |
| Speed | An optional minimum and maximum speed range filters tracks. |
| Direction | An optional direction filter uses a configured direction and uncertainty range. |
| Object age | A minimum age can exclude tracks until they have been observed long enough. |
| Hidden time | A maximum hidden time controls how long a temporarily unobserved track can remain part of the evaluation. |

Use SOPASair for the displayed units and the
[multiScan100 REST API reference](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/multiScan100/api-rest-openapi/) for
numeric constraints and enum values. The REST configuration uses
`EvaluationId` to associate a contour and criteria with an evaluation.

## Configure and Validate

1. Confirm that the sensor has firmware 2.5.0 or later and the **3D Object
   Detection Advanced** package.
2. In **Configuration > Basic settings**, turn off interlaced mode. Object
   evaluation is unavailable in interlaced mode; the sensor reports
   [error 211](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/troubleshooting/error-codes/).
3. Open the **Object Evaluation** application in SOPASair. Define the region
   of interest and choose the motion, size, speed, direction, and age criteria
   that match the application.
4. Activate the configured evaluation group. A group can be activated or
   deactivated through the REST API as well as the device interface.
5. Test representative objects and movements in the intended region. Confirm
   that qualifying tracks produce the expected result and that excluded tracks
   do not.
6. Monitor the application, group, configuration, and evaluation states
   described below.

## Read and Interpret Results

Use these read-only REST endpoints to check whether the application is
available, the group is active, and the evaluation result matches the scene.

<p class="table-caption" markdown>**Object Evaluation status endpoints:** REST path and returned status.</p>

| REST endpoint | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `GET /api/ObjectEvaluationApplicationState` | Application state: `0` DEACTIVATED, `1` ACTIVE, `2` CONFIGURING, or `3` ERROR. |
| `GET /api/ObjectEvaluationGroupState` | Activation state for configured groups: `0` NOT_CONFIGURED, `1` ACTIVE, or `2` INACTIVE. |
| `GET /api/ObjectEvaluationResult` | Results for configured evaluations. `EvaluationResultList` contains one state per evaluation. |
| `GET /api/ObjectEvaluationConfigState` | Reports whether active beam and evaluation limits are `0` OK, `1` WARNING, or `2` EXCEEDED. |

Each state in `EvaluationResultList` has a distinct meaning:

<p class="table-caption" markdown>**Evaluation result states:** numeric value and interpretation.</p>

| Value | State | Meaning |
| ---: | --- | --- |
| `0` | `NOT_CONFIGURED` | No evaluation is configured for this entry. |
| `1` | `INACTIVE` | The evaluation is configured but not active. |
| `2` | `FREE` | No qualifying object infringes the evaluation. |
| `3` | `DETECTING_INFRINGED` | The sensor is confirming an infringement. |
| `4` | `INFRINGED` | A qualifying object infringes the evaluation. |
| `5` | `DETECTING_FREE` | The sensor is confirming that the infringement has cleared. |

Treat `DETECTING_INFRINGED` and `DETECTING_FREE` as transitional states, not
stable results. The application state, group state, configuration state, and per-evaluation
result are separate. Check the relevant status endpoints when diagnosing an
unexpected output.

## Configure Through REST

The REST API provides operations to get and set each evaluation's contour and
criteria, and to activate or deactivate a group. The get/set contour and
configuration operations require at least the **Authorized Client** user
level. Review the request schemas and error codes in the
[multiScan100 REST API reference](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/multiScan100/api-rest-openapi/) before
writing configuration.

<p class="table-caption" markdown>**Object Evaluation configuration operations:** REST method and purpose.</p>

| REST operation | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `POST /api/GetObjectEvaluationContour` | Read an evaluation's polygon and lower/upper Z limits. |
| `POST /api/SetObjectEvaluationContour` | Set an evaluation's polygon and lower/upper Z limits. |
| `POST /api/GetObjectEvaluationConfiguration` | Read an evaluation's name and criteria. |
| `POST /api/SetObjectEvaluationConfiguration` | Set an evaluation's name and criteria. |
| `POST /api/ActivateObjectEvaluationGroup` | Activate or deactivate an evaluation group. |

The `Get...` operations above use HTTP `POST` with an evaluation ID in the
request body. Do not confuse them with the read-only `GET` status endpoints.
After changing settings, read them back and verify the live result in SOPASair.

## Configure Through CoLa

The same status variables and operations are available as CoLa telegrams, for
example for a PLC. See the
[Object Evaluation telegrams](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/multiScan100/api-cola-telegrams/#object-evaluation)
in the multiScan100 CoLa telegram listing for the structures and copyable
CoLa A and CoLa B examples.

`ActivateObjectEvaluationGroup` switches only groups with the activation type
Telegram. For a group with the activation type Always, the device confirms
the request, but the group stays active. Read `ObjectEvaluationGroupState`
to confirm the change. Changes made through CoLa or REST are lost on restart
unless you save them permanently.

# Perpendicular Distance Measurement on SICK LiDAR Sensors

> Review perpendicular-distance availability on LRS4000, multiScan100, and picoScan100, with a detailed picoScan100 configuration and API workflow.

Source: https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/on-device-applications/perpendicular-distance-measurement/

# Perpendicular Distance Measurement

Compatible with: LRS4000 multiScan100 picoScan100

Perpendicular distance evaluation measures object distances relative to a
reference line in the scan plane. Define a field and reference line in the
application; the sensor evaluates the points in that field and
reports the minimum and maximum perpendicular distances and the positions of
the corresponding measuring points.

*multiScan1xx: Perpendicular distance application demonstration.*

## Configure a Measurement

1. Open **Application > Perpendicular distance measurement** in SOPASair and
   add an evaluation group.
2. Draw the zone in which objects should be measured.
3. Set **Max. blanking size** and **Detection time** under Object detection to
   balance measurement stability and response time for the target.
4. Save the configuration to the device.
5. Check the live minimum and maximum distances and their measuring-point
   coordinates in the result list.

The evaluation runs on the sensor, so the host receives measurement results
without having to detect objects from the raw scan itself. See the
[SOPASair configuration walkthrough](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/picoScan100/graphical-user-interface/#perpendicular-distance-measurement)
for the interface details.

*picoScan100 example: Output a field's perpendicular distance after configuring the measurement field; use the interfaces below to read the results in your application.*

## Read Results

The REST endpoint `GET /api/perpendicularDistanceResult` returns a timestamp
and an `evaluations` array. Each result contains an evaluation ID, minimum and
maximum distance, and the 3D position of each corresponding measuring point.
The `evaluations` array is empty when no object is measured. The result is read-only; see the [picoScan100 REST API reference](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/picoScan100/api-rest-openapi/).

CoLa clients can poll `sRN perpendicularDistanceResult` for the current
measurement or subscribe with `sEN perpendicularDistanceResult` for event
updates. The telegram reports the shortest and furthest measuring point in
the range relative to the reference plane. See the
[picoScan100 CoLa Telegram Listing](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/picoScan100/api-cola-telegrams/).

## Configure over the API (picoScan100)

REST and CoLa expose every variable needed to create, change, and delete a
perpendicular distance evaluation without SOPASair. The following workflow
applies to picoScan150 with firmware V2.3.3. Some of these variables are
not listed in the published OpenAPI file, but can be read and written as REST
variables (`GET` / `POST /api/<Variable>`).

A perpendicular distance evaluation has two parts, as in SOPASair:

<p class="table-caption" markdown>**Configure over the API (picoScan100):** part, variables, and content.</p>

| Part | Variables | Content |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Object detection | `EvalNNN`, `VolumeNNN` | Detection parameters (blanking mode, minimum object size, detection time) and the field in which objects are measured |
| Reference line | `perpDistNNN` | Normal vector of the line in the scan plane and its signed distance from the sensor, in mm |

To create an evaluation, log in as **Authorized client** or **Service** and
write the variables in this order, using the same slot number `NNN`
throughout:

1. Set the slot to perpendicular distance: write `EvaluationGroupType` with
   all 48 values and `1` at the slot position (`0` = field evaluation).
2. Write `EvalNNN` with `VolumeList = [NNN]`.
3. Write the field polygon directly to `VolumeNNN`. Do not use
   `SetFieldEvaluationContour` here: it returns success for perpendicular
   distance slots but is not reliable for them.
4. Write the reference line to `perpDistNNN`. The normal vector sets the
   orientation, for example `(1, 0, 0)` for a line across the forward
   direction, and the distance sets its position. Because the picoScan100 is a
   2D sensor, the `z` component is always `0`. The no-data mode sets the
   output when no object is measured: `0` zero, `1` hold the last value, or
   `2` a user-defined substitution distance.
5. Add the group to `EvaluationGroupMapping` with `EvalIds = [NNN]`. The whole
   array is replaced on every write, so include every group you want to keep.
6. Call `WriteEeprom` and wait about 1 s before reading the result.

Keep in mind:

- Perpendicular distance groups need their own slots; they cannot share a
  slot with a field evaluation group.
- If the field is missing (empty `VolumeList` or empty `VolumeNNN`) or the
  group references no evaluation, the device reports a recoverable error
  (`DeviceStatus` = `7` instead of `3`) and the result stays empty.
- Perpendicular distance results are not assigned to digital outputs; read
  them from `perpendicularDistanceResult`.
- Group activation (`ALWAYS`, `INPUTS`, `TELEGRAM`) and `ActivateEvaluationGroup`
  work as for [field evaluation](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/on-device-applications/field-evaluation/#configure-over-the-api).

To delete the evaluation, remove the group from `EvaluationGroupMapping`,
clear `EvalNNN`, `VolumeNNN`, and `perpDistNNN`, set the slot in
`EvaluationGroupType` back to `0`, and call `WriteEeprom`.

For output and evaluation-group concepts shared with field evaluation, see
[Field Evaluation](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/on-device-applications/field-evaluation/).


---

# LiDAR Contamination Indication: Monitor the Optics Cover

> Monitor dirt on the optics cover of LRS4000, multiScan100, multiScan200, and picoScan100 sensors by sector, and read or configure contamination results via REST.

Source: https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/on-device-applications/contamination-indication/

# Contamination Indication

Compatible with: LRS4000 multiScan100 multiScan200 picoScan100

Contamination indication monitors the sensor's optics cover for dirt that
could reduce measurement quality. It evaluates contamination per sector of the
optics cover, so maintenance can target the affected area before the optics
become too dirty. The number of sectors depends on the device. The SOPASair
sector display shows where contamination is accumulating, with overall states
such as **Clean**, **Minor**, **Heavy**, and **Blocked**.

![SOPASair contamination indication tile with status, sector display, and configuration settings](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/assets/multiScan200/img/sopasair-configuration-contamination-indication-tile.png)
*Contamination indication tile in SOPASair, captured live from a multiScan270: overall status, sector display, and configuration.*

Configure the sensitivity, response time, warning threshold, and active
sectors for the installation. The device can expose the result through its
GUI and REST API; depending on configuration, it can also be monitored
through CoLa or mapped to digital outputs. The warning and error behavior,
and whether blocked sectors count as errors, are configurable. Use the
indication as a maintenance signal and inspect and clean the optics according
to the product documentation.

All contamination settings and results are available through the REST API.
The endpoints are listed under **Contamination Indication** in the
[LRS4000 REST API](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/LRS4000/api-rest-openapi/),
[multiScan100 REST API](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/multiScan100/api-rest-openapi/),
[multiScan200 REST API](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/multiScan200/api-rest-openapi/), and
[picoScan100 REST API](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/picoScan100/api-rest-openapi/) references.

Writes require the Authorized Client user level and challenge-response
authentication. Persist configuration changes with `WriteEeprom`; otherwise,
they may be lost after a power cycle.

picoScan100 CoLa clients can read configuration and sector data and subscribe
to event-driven contamination updates. See the
[picoScan100 CoLa Telegram Listing](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/picoScan100/api-cola-telegrams/).
For the interface walkthrough, see
[Contamination Indication in SOPASair](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/picoScan100/graphical-user-interface/#contamination-indication).

*picoScan100 example: Compare optics-cover contamination states with the sector indications described above.*

# 3D Scan Recording: On-Device Point Clouds from a 2D LiDAR

> Record a 3D point cloud on an LRS4000 or picoScan150 that rotates on an axis, using the IMU or an encoder, and download it as a PCD file.

Source: https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/on-device-applications/3d-scan-recording/

# 3D Scan Recording

Compatible with: LRS4000 picoScan100

3D scan recording turns a rotating 2D LiDAR into a 3D scanner without host-side
geometry code. While the sensor rotates on an axis, it combines consecutive 2D
scans with the rotation angle and stores one point cloud as a `.pcd` file on
the device. The angle comes from the built-in IMU or from an encoder on the
axis. Open the result in [CloudCompare](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/visualization/cloudcompare/).

The device keeps only the most recent point cloud, and there is no continuous
3D output. For continuous 3D data or custom transforms, process the scans on
the host as described in [3D With 2D LiDARs](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/integration-notes/3d-with-2d-lidars/).

![3D scan recording interface](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/assets/picoScan100/img/sopasair-application-pointcloud.png)
*Live capture of the 3D scan recording interface on a picoScan100.*

## Record in SOPASair

1. Mount the sensor so its scan plane sweeps the area of interest as it rotates.
2. Open **Application → 3D scan recording**, select the rotation source (IMU or
   encoder), and enter the sensor offset from the rotation axis.
3. Start the recording, rotate the sensor through the sweep, and stop the
   recording.
4. Download the point cloud when saving is complete.

## Record over the REST API

Writing parameters and calling methods requires
[challenge-response authentication](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/configuration/rest-interface/#challenge-response-authentication).

<p class="table-caption" markdown>**Record over the REST API:** parameter and values.</p>

| Parameter           | Values                                                         |
| ------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `ScanMergerEnabled` | `true` / `false`                                               |
| `ScanMergerSource`  | `0` IMU, `1` ENCODER                                           |
| `ScanMergeTrigger`  | `0` METHOD; on the LRS4000 also `1` DIGITAL_INPUT              |
| `RotationOffset`    | `{x, y, z}` in mm: sensor offset from the rotation axis        |

1. Write the parameters and persist them with `POST /api/WriteEeprom`.
2. picoScan150 only: `POST /api/ResetScanMergeView` to clear the previous recording.
3. `POST /api/StartScanMerge` and move the axis through the sweep. With
   `ScanMergeTrigger = 1`, a digital input starts and stops the recording instead.
4. `POST /api/StopScanMerge`.
5. picoScan150 only: poll `GET /api/MergeSaving` until it changes from `true` back to `false`.
6. Download the point cloud. On the picoScan150, use port 80 outside `/api/`:
   `curl http://192.168.0.1/cloud.pcd -o cloud.pcd`. On the LRS4000, download it
   in SOPASair under **Application → 3D scan recording**.

The endpoints are listed in the [LRS4000](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/LRS4000/api-rest-openapi/) and
[picoScan100](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/picoScan100/api-rest-openapi/) REST API references. For a
complete example, see the [House 3D Capture](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/beginner-projects/house-3d-capture/)
project.

# LiDAR Data Streaming: Compact, MSGPACK, LMDscandata

> Choose a SICK LiDAR data format or event interface for measurement streams, notifications, and on-sensor filtering.

Source: https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/data-streaming/

# Choose a Data Streaming Option

* [Compact Format](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/data-streaming/compact-format/): start here for new integrations needing low-bandwidth, low-latency binary scan, IMU, and encoder data; the parser must know the layout.
* [MSGPACK Format](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/data-streaming/msgpack-format/): self-describing scan data parsed with standard libraries; useful for quick Python prototypes.
* [LMDscandata Format](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/data-streaming/lmdscandata-format/): CoLa scan telegrams for PLCs and existing CoLa integrations; less suited to high data rates.
* [WebSocket Events](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/data-streaming/websocket-events/): low-latency JSON notifications for changing device values, state, and results—not scan data.
* [Filter Details](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/data-streaming/filter-details/): configure on-sensor filters to reduce bandwidth or suppress unwanted points; some filters affect output rate or represent filtered points as zero.

Format availability, transport, and filters depend on the device family,
variant, and firmware. Filters apply to the supported measurement formats.
Use the [Bandwidth Calculator](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/data-streaming/compact-format/#bandwidth-calculator) to
estimate Compact scan frame sizes, segment counts, and traffic for your output
and filter settings.

<p class="table-caption" markdown>**Choose a Data Streaming Option:** device family, Compact, MSGPACK, LMDscandata, and WebSocket events.</p>

| Device family | Compact | MSGPACK | LMDscandata | WebSocket events |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| LRS4000 | Yes | No | Yes | No |
| multiScan100 | Yes | Yes | No | No |
| multiScan200 | Yes | No | No | Yes |
| picoScan100 | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes |

<figure class="setup-diagram" aria-label="Interfaces between a customer application and a SICK LiDAR sensor">
  <div class="setup-diagram__app">Customer Application</div>
  <div class="setup-diagram__box setup-diagram__box--rest">REST</div>
  <div class="setup-diagram__box setup-diagram__box--websocket">WebSocket</div>
  <div class="setup-diagram__box setup-diagram__box--compact">Compact</div>
  <div class="setup-diagram__label">Configuration</div>
  <div class="setup-diagram__label">Notifications</div>

</figure>

See [REST Interface](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/configuration/rest-interface/) for configuration requests.
