# SICK LiDAR: Generate Parsers with Kaitai Struct

> Generate Compact data parsers for SICK LiDAR sensors using Kaitai Struct, with a browser-based workflow or the command-line compiler.

Source: https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/integration-notes/kaitai-struct-parsers/

# Kaitai Struct Parsers

Compatible with: LRS4000 multiScan100 multiScan200 picoScan100

<div class="tool-intro" markdown>

![Kaitai Struct](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/assets/integration-notes/kaitai-struct-logo.png)
[Kaitai Struct](https://kaitai.io/) generates parsing code from a binary-format description. Use SICK's [KaitaiStructDescriptions](https://github.com/SICKAG/KaitaiStructDescriptions) to build a [Compact](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/data-streaming/compact-format/) parser in Python, C++, C#, Java, Go, or another supported language instead of implementing the byte layout yourself.

</div>

## What Is Kaitai Struct?

A `.ksy` file describes a binary format in YAML: field names, data types, byte order, repeated structures, and conditions. The compiler turns that description into parser classes for your chosen language. The same description can therefore serve applications written in different languages without maintaining separate byte-offset logic.

The Web IDE combines a hex view with a parsed field tree. Load a captured telegram to explore the structure before adding the generated code to your application.

## Compact Frame and Payloads

The definitions are in the repository's `formats` directory. Start with `compact_frame.ksy`: it reads the outer frame and selects the payload definition using `telegram_type`. Keep the other `.ksy` files alongside it because the frame imports them. The definitions cover scan, IMU, ambient-light, and encoder telegrams; availability depends on the sensor.

All telegrams have the following outer frame. Multi-byte numbers are little-endian.

<p class="table-caption" markdown>**Compact Frame:** fields in transmission order, size, and purpose.</p>

| Field            | Size     | Purpose                                                 |
| ---------------- | -------- | ------------------------------------------------------- |
| `start_of_frame` | 4 bytes  | Start marker: `02 02 02 02`                             |
| `telegram_type`  | 4 bytes  | Selects the payload definition                          |
| `payload`        | Variable | Scan, IMU, ambient-light, or encoder data               |
| `checksum`       | 4 bytes  | CRC32 over the start marker, telegram type, and payload |

The [frame definition](https://github.com/SICKAG/KaitaiStructDescriptions/blob/public/formats/compact_frame.ksy) imports these payload definitions:

<p class="table-caption" markdown>**Payload Definitions:** telegram type, content, and supported devices.</p>

| Type | Definition                                                                                                                                               | Devices                            |
| ---- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------- |
| 1    | [Scan data, spherical coordinates](https://github.com/SICKAG/KaitaiStructDescriptions/blob/public/formats/type_1_primary_data_spherical_coordinates.ksy) | LRS4000, multiScan100, picoScan100 |
| 2    | [IMU](https://github.com/SICKAG/KaitaiStructDescriptions/blob/public/formats/type_2_imu.ksy)                                                             | multiScan100, picoScan100          |
| 3    | [Ambient light](https://github.com/SICKAG/KaitaiStructDescriptions/blob/public/formats/type_3_ambient_light.ksy)                                         | multiScan200                       |
| 4    | [Encoder](https://github.com/SICKAG/KaitaiStructDescriptions/blob/public/formats/type_4_encoder.ksy)                                                     | picoScan150                        |
| 6    | [multiScan200 scan data](https://github.com/SICKAG/KaitaiStructDescriptions/blob/public/formats/type_6_primary_data_multiscan200.ksy)                    | multiScan200                       |
| 7    | [IMU with standard header](https://github.com/SICKAG/KaitaiStructDescriptions/blob/public/formats/type_7_imu_standard_header.ksy)                        | multiScan200                       |

Types 3, 4, 6, and 7 use the shared [standard header](https://github.com/SICKAG/KaitaiStructDescriptions/blob/public/formats/compact_header.ksy). Types 1 and 2 have their own layouts. Use the linked definitions for the complete field layout and the operating instructions for device-specific output settings.

## Generate in the Web IDE

1. Download the repository using **Code > Download ZIP** and extract it.
2. Open the [Kaitai Web IDE](https://ide.kaitai.io/).
3. Import the `.ksy` files from `formats`, including `compact_frame.ksy` and its dependencies.
4. Right-click `compact_frame.ksy` in the file tree, select **Generate Parser**, and choose your target language.
5. Save the generated modules and add them to your application together with the matching [Kaitai Struct runtime library](https://kaitai.io/#download).

To inspect a capture, load a `.bin` file containing one complete Compact telegram into the hex view. Use only the application payload, including the Compact start marker and checksum, not a complete Ethernet packet or a PCAP file.

## Generate from the Command Line

Install the [Kaitai Struct compiler](https://kaitai.io/#download), including its Java prerequisite, and add `kaitai-struct-compiler` to your `PATH`. Clone the definitions and generate a Python parser:

```powershell
git clone https://github.com/SICKAG/KaitaiStructDescriptions.git
Set-Location KaitaiStructDescriptions
kaitai-struct-compiler -t python --outdir generated formats\compact_frame.ksy
```

The compiler writes `compact_frame.py` and the imported payload modules to `generated`. Keep those modules together. For another language, change the `-t` value; run `kaitai-struct-compiler --help` to list the supported targets.

For example, generate C# or C++/STL code with:

```powershell
kaitai-struct-compiler -t csharp --outdir generated-csharp formats\compact_frame.ksy
kaitai-struct-compiler -t cpp_stl --outdir generated-cpp formats\compact_frame.ksy
```

For Python, install the runtime in your application's environment:

```powershell
python -m pip install kaitaistruct
```

The runtime reads the binary data; the compiler is needed only when generating or updating the parser. Other target languages need their corresponding runtime library.

Warnings suggesting `num_*` names for count fields are style warnings, not parsing errors.

## Use the Generated Parser

Pass one complete Compact telegram to the generated `CompactFrame` parser. Read `telegram_type` first, then access the corresponding `payload` fields. See [Compact Format](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/data-streaming/compact-format/) for the telegram types, field conventions, and conversion to Cartesian coordinates.

### Scan Data

For type 1, `payload.header` contains the telegram version and counter. `payload.module` holds the modules; each module has metadata and beam data. The metadata describes the number of beams, layers, and echoes, the acquisition times, and the elevation and azimuth angles.

This Python example reads one complete Compact telegram from `telegram.bin`,
for example a UDP payload saved with **File > Export Packet Bytes** in Wireshark,
and prints every echo:

```python
import sys

sys.path.insert(0, "generated")  # folder written by kaitai-struct-compiler
from compact_frame import CompactFrame

with open("telegram.bin", "rb") as file:  # one complete Compact telegram
    frame = CompactFrame.from_bytes(file.read())

if frame.telegram_type == 1:
    for module in frame.payload.module:
        meta = module.metadata
        print("frame", meta.frame_number, "beams", meta.number_of_beams_per_scan)
        for beam in module.beams:
            for line in beam.lines:
                for echo in line.echos:
                    distance = echo.distance if meta.data_content_echos.distance else None
                    rssi = echo.rssi if meta.data_content_echos.rssi else None
                    print(distance, rssi)
```

Example code: [MIT License](https://opensource.org/license/mit), © 2026 SICK AG. Provided as is, without warranty. Test it before you use it with a machine or in production.

The generated `distance` property applies the version-4 scaling factor and returns millimeters. `distance_raw` is the unscaled value. Check the content flags before accessing optional fields. Combine distance with the layer elevation and beam azimuth for point-cloud reconstruction; see [Type 1: Scan Data](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/data-streaming/compact-format/#type-1-scan-data).

### IMU Data

Type 2 has a fixed-size payload without repeated scan modules. Its fields are available directly under `frame.payload`. Which measurements are usable depends on the sensor.

<p class="table-caption" markdown>**IMU Fields:** generated payload fields and their meaning.</p>

| Field                             | Meaning                          |
| --------------------------------- | -------------------------------- |
| `acceleration.x`, `.y`, `.z`      | Acceleration in m/s²             |
| `angular_velocity.x`, `.y`, `.z`  | Angular velocity in rad/s        |
| `orientation.w`, `.x`, `.y`, `.z` | Orientation quaternion           |
| `timestamp`                       | Sensor timestamp in microseconds |

For multiScan200, select type 7 instead. It has the standard header before the IMU measurements.

### Encoder Data

Type 4 links an external encoder reading to the scan through `frame_number`. The common header is under `frame.payload.header`; encoder values are directly under `frame.payload`.

<p class="table-caption" markdown>**Encoder Fields:** generated payload fields and their meaning.</p>

| Field                                                                  | Meaning                                                      |
| ---------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `frame_number`                                                         | Identifies the corresponding scan frame                      |
| `tick_count`                                                           | Current encoder count                                        |
| `tick_count_at_reference_signal_1`, `tick_count_at_reference_signal_2` | Counts captured at reference signals                         |
| `speed`                                                                | Speed in units/s according to the configured conversion rate |
| `tick_count_timestamp`                                                 | Time of the last count change                                |
| `timestamp_of_reference_signal_1`, `timestamp_of_reference_signal_2`   | Times of the reference-signal events                         |

For an application example, see [3D With 2D LiDARs](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/integration-notes/3d-with-2d-lidars/).

*picoScan100 example: Receive Compact data in C# with Kaitai Struct after reviewing the generated parser. Your application still needs the reception and validation handling described below.*

## Reception and Validation

The parser does not receive data from the sensor. Your application must handle the connection and telegram boundaries:

* For UDP, receive the complete datagram payload. IP fragments must be reassembled before parsing.
* For TCP, collect bytes until a complete Compact telegram is available. A single socket read can contain part of a telegram or several telegrams.
* Validate the CRC32 separately. The frame definition reads the checksum but does not verify it.
* Handle truncated or unsupported telegrams explicitly. Check the sensor's operating instructions and firmware compatibility before using decoded values.

To compare your decoded values with a capture, use the [Compact Wireshark dissector](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/data-streaming/compact-format/#wireshark-dissector). If you prefer a library that also handles reception, see [Coding Tools & Examples](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/integration-notes/coding-tools-and-examples/).

# Use SICK LiDAR Data in MATLAB via ROS 2

> Subscribe to picoScan100 PointCloud2 data in MATLAB with the ROS Toolbox over native ROS 2 (DDS), without a SICK driver.

Source: https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/integration-notes/matlab-integration/

# MATLAB Integration

Compatible with: multiScan200 picoScan100

<div class="tool-intro" markdown>

![MATLAB](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/assets/integration-notes/matlab-logo.png)
MATLAB ROS Toolbox can subscribe directly to native ROS 2 data from
multiScan200 or picoScan100 through DDS. No SICK ROS driver or bridge is
required. The example below uses picoScan100 point-cloud data on
`/cloud/all_points` as `sensor_msgs/PointCloud2` with the default ROS domain
ID `0`.

</div>

## Validated Setup

<p class="table-caption" markdown>**Validated Setup:** component and version or setting.</p>

| Component | Version / setting |
| --- | --- |
| Operating system | Windows 11 |
| MATLAB | R2025b with ROS Toolbox |
| ROS 2 / DDS | Kilted with CycloneDDS |
| ROS domain ID | `0` (device default) |

All DDS participants must use the same domain ID as the sensor. Ensure that the sensor's native ROS 2 interface is enabled and that the computer firewall allows DDS traffic. See [Native ROS 2](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/integration-notes/ros-integration/#native-ros-2) for sensor-side setup.

## Receive PointCloud2 Data

The following script creates a MATLAB ROS 2 node, lists visible topics, and prints the number of points received on `/cloud/all_points`.

```matlab
node = ros2node("/matlab_cloud_counter");

disp("Available ROS 2 topics:");
disp(ros2("topic", "list"));

% Keep the subscriber handle alive until after message reception.
sub = ros2subscriber( ...
    node, ...
    "/cloud/all_points", ...
    "sensor_msgs/PointCloud2", ...
    @onPointCloud); %#ok<NASGU>

disp("Subscribed to /cloud/all_points");

t0 = tic;
while toc(t0) < 10
    pause(0.1);
end

clear sub node
disp("Finished.");

function onPointCloud(msg)
    pointCount = double(msg.width) * double(msg.height);
    fprintf("PointCloud received: %d points\n", pointCount);
end
```

Example code: [MIT License](https://opensource.org/license/mit), © 2026 SICK AG. Provided as is, without warranty. Test it before you use it with a machine or in production.

## Visualize Live Data

Open **Apps** > **ROS 2 Data Analyzer**, choose **Open** > **Live Network Data**, select **Live ROS 2 network data**, and set the ROS domain ID to `0`. Create a PointCloud Visualizer, choose `/cloud/all_points`, then select **Start**.

## Verify Connectivity

Use the ROS 2 CLI independently of MATLAB to verify that DDS data is present:

```sh
ros2 topic echo /cloud/all_points
```

If no data is visible, confirm the native ROS 2 interface configuration,
firewall rules, DDS compatibility, and ROS domain ID. On multiScan200 and on
picoScan100 from firmware V2.3.1, the sensor domain ID is configurable
(`rosDomainId`); make sure MATLAB uses the same value.

# PLC Integration of SICK LiDAR Sensors via CoLa B over TCP

> Connect SICK LiDAR sensors to Siemens, Beckhoff, Mitsubishi, or Rockwell PLCs using CoLa B over TCP port 2112: framing, polling, telegrams, and troubleshooting.

Source: https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/integration-notes/plc-integration/

# PLC Integration

Compatible with: LRS4000 multiScan100 multiScan200 picoScan100

Use the CoLa command protocol over a TCP/IP socket to receive measurement,
field-evaluation, and I/O data from SICK LiDAR sensors on Siemens, Beckhoff,
Mitsubishi, or Rockwell PLCs. SICK does not provide maintained PLC function
blocks for the product families on this page; implement a small
length-prefixed receive routine using the controller's native TCP socket API.

## Interface and Approach

For PLC applications, use CoLa B on TCP port `2112`. Its length-prefixed telegrams are easier to process than CoLa A on port `2111`. Open one bidirectional TCP connection from the PLC to the sensor, keep it open, and poll the required values by sending an `sRN` request and reading the matching `sRA` response on that same connection.

<p class="table-caption" markdown>**Interface and Approach:** interface, transport, and suitable use.</p>

| Interface | Transport | Suitable use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| CoLa A / B | TCP 2111 / 2112 | PLC commands and telegram access |
| Compact / MSGPACK | UDP | High-rate scan streams to a computer or edge device |
| REST API | HTTP(S) 80 / 443 | Configuration, diagnostics, and firmware updates |

Configure the sensor once through SOPASair: use a fixed IP address reachable from the PLC, configure scan profiles, field-evaluation groups, and I/O, then export a parameter backup. Do not repeatedly configure the sensor from cyclic PLC logic. Enable LMDscandata only when the PLC requires distance data.

## Polling and CoLa B Framing

The PLC is the client and connects to `<device-ip>:2112`. Send a request, receive one complete telegram, parse it, and reconnect after an error or timeout.

```text
connect(device_ip, 2112)
loop:
  send(frame("sRN LMDscandata"))
  reply = receive_one_telegram()
  parse(reply)
```

Every CoLa B telegram has this layout:

<p class="table-caption" markdown>**Polling and CoLa B Framing:** field, size, and value.</p>

| Field | Size | Value |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Start | 4 bytes | `02 02 02 02` |
| Length | 4 bytes | Big-endian payload length |
| Payload | N bytes | Command type, name, and data |
| Checksum | 1 byte | XOR of all payload bytes |

TCP is a byte stream: a receive operation can return a partial telegram or several telegrams. Buffer incoming bytes; after at least eight bytes are available, validate the start sequence, read the big-endian length, then wait for exactly `8 + length + 1` bytes. Validate the XOR checksum, consume one telegram, and retain any remaining bytes for the next call.

To validate this logic on a PC before porting it to the PLC, use this Python function on the received bytes:

```python
def next_telegram(buffer: bytearray) -> bytes | None:
    header = b"\x02\x02\x02\x02"
    if len(buffer) < len(header):
        return None
    if buffer[:4] != header:
        start = buffer.find(header)
        if start < 0:
            del buffer[:-3]  # preserve a possible partial header
            return None
        del buffer[:start]
    if len(buffer) < 8:
        return None
    length = int.from_bytes(buffer[4:8], "big")
    if len(buffer) < 8 + length + 1:
        return None  # wait for more bytes
    payload, checksum = bytes(buffer[8:8 + length]), buffer[8 + length]
    del buffer[:8 + length + 1]  # keep the remaining bytes for the next call
    xor = 0
    for byte in payload:
        xor ^= byte
    return payload if xor == checksum else None
```

Example code: [MIT License](https://opensource.org/license/mit), © 2026 SICK AG. Provided as is, without warranty. Test it before you use it with a machine or in production.

## Common Telegrams

<p class="table-caption" markdown>**Common Telegrams:** telegram, purpose, and PLC consideration.</p>

| Telegram | Purpose | PLC consideration |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `SCdevicestate` | Device health | Poll slowly and invalidate dependent values when not ready. |
| `LMDscandata` | Distance and optional RSSI data | Reduce it below the network MTU where possible. |
| `perpendicularDistanceResult` | Minimum and maximum distance to a field boundary where the device supports perpendicular distance | Its value can remain unchanged after the field is clear; gate it with field state. |
| `FieldEvaluationResult` | Free/occupied result for each evaluation group | Map each group index to the configured physical zone. |
| `LIDinputstate` / `LIDoutputstate` | Digital I/O states | Use to mirror sensor I/O in the PLC process image. |

Request each with `sRN <name>` and parse the `sRA <name> ...` response. Confirm the exact payload layout, byte offsets, and data types against the Telegram Listing for the installed firmware.

To keep `LMDscandata` manageable, use only the required echo, disable RSSI when not needed, restrict the scan angle, and select the coarsest acceptable angular resolution. A small telegram reduces PLC processing load and TCP segmentation.

## Controller Notes

<p class="table-caption" markdown>**Controller Notes:** controller and TCP mechanism.</p>

| Controller | TCP mechanism |
| --- | --- |
| Siemens S7-1500 / S7-1200 | Open User Communication: `TCON_IP_v4`, `TSEND_C`, and `TRCV_C`; use variable-length receives. |
| Siemens S7-300 / S7-400 | CP module with `AG_SEND` / `AG_RECV` and FB54 TCP. |
| Beckhoff TwinCAT 3 | Tc2_TcpIp: `FB_SocketConnect`, `FB_SocketSend`, and `FB_SocketReceive`. |
| Mitsubishi GX Works2 / iQ | Ethernet socket services: `SP_SOCOPEN`, `SP_SOCSND`, `SP_SOCRCV`, and `SP_SOCCLOSE`. |
| Rockwell / Allen-Bradley | Raw TCP socket object with MSG instructions for connect, write, read, and close. |

The transport API differs, but the CoLa B framing and receive-buffer logic are identical for every PLC.

## Troubleshooting

<p class="table-caption" markdown>**Troubleshooting:** symptom, cause, and action.</p>

| Symptom | Cause | Action |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Connection refused on `2112` | Incorrect network settings or CoLa B disabled | Verify the sensor IP/subnet and CoLa B configuration. |
| No response | Malformed request or wrong telegram name | Validate start bytes, length, XOR checksum, and case-sensitive command name. |
| `sFA` error response | Unsupported or unavailable variable | Check the [CoLa error codes](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/configuration/cola-interface/#cola-error-codes), Telegram Listing, and firmware version. |
| Receive never completes | Fixed-size receive or TCP fragmentation | Buffer data and use the length field to determine the complete frame. |
| Misaligned data | Concatenated frames or unconsumed bytes | Consume exactly one frame and retain the buffer remainder. |
| Frozen values | Repeated scan or stale perpendicular-distance result | Verify scan counter/timestamp and use `FieldEvaluationResult` to validate the distance. |

# SICK LiDAR ROS 2 Integration: Native ROS 2 and sick_scan_xd

> Get SICK LiDAR data into ROS 2 with native ROS 2 on selected families or the sick_scan_xd host driver, with setup, topics, limitations, and CPU notes.

Source: https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/integration-notes/ros-integration/

# ROS Integration

Compatible with: LRS4000 multiScan100 multiScan200 picoScan100

<div class="tool-intro" markdown>

![ROS 2](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/assets/integration-notes/ros2-logo.png)
There are two ways to get LiDAR data into ROS 2: the sensor publishes ROS 2
messages itself (native ROS 2), or a driver on the host receives sensor data
and publishes the messages (`sick_scan_xd`). Both deliver standard ROS 2
messages to your nodes. The difference is which product families they cover
and where decoding and publishing run.

</div>

<div class="center-table-headers" markdown="1">

<p class="table-caption" markdown>**ROS Integration:** integration path and compatible devices.</p>

| Integration path | Compatible with |
| --- | --- |
| Native ROS 2 | multiScan200, picoScan100 |
| `sick_scan_xd` | LRS4000, multiScan100, picoScan100 |

</div>

The LRS4000 and multiScan100 do not support native ROS 2. Use `sick_scan_xd`
for these families.

<p class="table-caption" markdown>**ROS Integration:** option, what it is, advantages, trade-offs, and best fit.</p>

| Option | What it is | Advantages | Trade-offs | Best fit |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Native ROS 2](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/integration-notes/ros-integration/#native-ros-2) | The sensor firmware assembles the scan segments and publishes ROS 2 messages over DDS. | No driver on the host; lower host CPU load; hardware timestamps; any number of subscribers and other DDS clients can receive the data directly. | Cyclone DDS is the specified middleware; uses more network bandwidth than Compact; no IMU or diagnostics topics; configuration stays outside ROS 2; the picoScan150 needs a license. | ROS 2 systems where host CPU matters, for example navigation or SLAM on embedded computers. |
| [sick_scan_xd](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/integration-notes/ros-integration/#sick_scan_xd) | A ROS 2 driver on the host receives data through the driver-supported sensor protocol, assembles the scans, and publishes the messages. | Publishes `PointCloud2`, `LaserScan`, and IMU messages where supported; decoding is under host-side control; supports recording to rosbag files. | Decoding and publishing use host CPU; the driver must be installed and maintained on the host. | Applications that need IMU topics, LRS4000 or multiScan100 integration, or host-side control over decoding. |

## Native ROS 2

Compatible with: multiScan200 picoScan100

The product supports native ROS 2 communication via the DDS (Data Distribution Service) protocol. This enables efficient real-time transmission of measured data without additional drivers and with minimum delay time. The data is output directly in ROS 2-compatible formats.

- Filter settings in the product have a direct effect on the published data.
- Subscribed topics are published even if no measurement points are available. It is therefore recommended that you only subscribe to required topics.
- If the static IP address is changed, a restart of the device is required to output the topics correctly.

### Quick Start

1. Verify the ROS 2 with middleware Cyclone DDS is installed. Install the Eclipse Cyclone DDS middleware using the [Cyclone DDS installation instructions](https://docs.ros.org/en/kilted/Installation/DDS-Implementations/Working-with-Eclipse-CycloneDDS.html).
2. Enable **Native ROS 2 (DDS)** in the device web interface, open **Application → Data output** and set **Measurement data output format** to **Native ROS 2 (DDS)**.
3. Create a Cyclone DDS configuration file and set `NetworkInterfaceAddress` to the IP address of the host interface connected to the sensor, here `192.168.0.100`. See the [Cyclone DDS configuration reference](https://cyclonedds.io/docs/cyclonedds/latest/config/index.html) for additional options.

    ```xml
    <?xml version="1.0" encoding="utf-8"?>
    <CycloneDDS
      xmlns="https://cdds.io/config"
      xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
      xsi:schemaLocation="https://cdds.io/config https://raw.githubusercontent.com/eclipse-cyclonedds/cyclonedds/master/etc/cyclonedds.xsd">
      <Domain>
        <General>
          <NetworkInterfaceAddress>192.168.0.100</NetworkInterfaceAddress>
        </General>
      </Domain>
    </CycloneDDS>
    ```

4. Start `rviz2` and add one of the published topics.

The picoScan150 requires firmware V2.2.1 or later and an activated native ROS 2 license (`PICOSCAN RosConnect`). picoScan150 PRO versions (part numbers 1134610 and 1142273) are delivered with this license pre-installed. If the license is missing, contact SICK. See [LiDAR License Activation](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/shared-features/license-activation/) for the official activation instructions.

The picoScan120 requires firmware V2.2.1 or later. The latest firmware and update instructions for both devices are available from the [SICK firmware download](https://www.sick.com/de/en/downloads/media/swp680096).

![picoScan150 native ROS 2 license](https://support.sick.com/api/data/v9.2/msdyn_knowledgearticleimages(e84df29d-3542-f111-88b4-00224880a9a4)/msdyn_blobfile/$value?w=1800px)
*picoScan150 native ROS 2 license.*

On Windows, DDS discovery requires the sensor adapter to use the Private network profile; see [Getting Started](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/getting-started/#connect-the-sensor).

The ROS 2 domain ID on the host (`ROS_DOMAIN_ID`) must match the device. The default is `0`; it can be changed with `rosDomainId` (0-232) or in SOPASair (multiScan200; picoScan100 from firmware V2.3.1). DDS/RTPS discovery must be able to reach the sensor interface. Native ROS 2 publishes data only; configure the sensor through the REST API, CoLa, or the web interface.

### Visualize the Point Cloud

Start `rviz2` with the configuration file from Quick Start step 3:

=== "Linux"

    Source ROS 2, select Cyclone DDS, set the configuration file, and start `rviz2`:

    ```bash
    . /opt/ros/<distro>/setup.bash  # for example kilted
    export RMW_IMPLEMENTATION=rmw_cyclonedds_cpp
    export CYCLONEDDS_URI="file://$HOME/CycloneDDS/my-config.xml"
    rviz2
    ```

    In `rviz2`, add `/cloud/all_points` or a scan topic. Set **Fixed Frame** to `world`, or to the frame configured on the device.

=== "Windows"

    In a Windows command prompt, source ROS 2, select Cyclone DDS, set the configuration file, and start `rviz2`:

    ```bat
    call C:\dev\ros2_<distro>\local_setup.bat
    set RMW_IMPLEMENTATION=rmw_cyclonedds_cpp
    set CYCLONEDDS_URI=file://%USERPROFILE%/cyclonedds.xml
    rviz2
    ```

    In `rviz2`, add `/cloud/all_points` or a scan topic. Set **Fixed Frame** to `world`, or to the frame configured on the device.

### Limitations and Trade-Offs

Native ROS 2 is a sensor-to-host data publisher, not a complete ROS 2 control
interface:

- **No ROS diagnostics topic:** Device health and diagnosis are not exposed as
  a diagnostics topic in the ROS 2 graph. Use the device web interface for
  diagnosis and troubleshooting. See the [SOPASair overview](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/visualization/sopasair/).
- **Configuration stays outside ROS 2:** The interface does not expose sensor
  parameters, services, or actions. Configure scan profiles, field of view,
  filters, and other device settings through the web interface, REST API, or
  CoLa; they cannot be set as ROS parameters or from a ROS 2 launch file.
- **Use CycloneDDS:** Native ROS 2 is specified for CycloneDDS as the ROS
  middleware (RMW) on the host. Other RMW implementations and custom DDS
  environments are not validated. If you use one,
  test discovery and communication with your device firmware and ROS
  distribution.
- **Account for network load:** Native ROS 2 uses more network
  bandwidth than Compact over UDP. The device publishes its available ROS
  topics concurrently, and topics can continue to be published when a scan
  contains no measurement points. Subscribe only to topics the application
  needs, monitor network utilization at the selected scan configuration, and
  consider Compact if bandwidth is constrained.
- **Publisher changes follow firmware releases:** The DDS publisher runs in
  the sensor firmware, rather than a host-side driver. Publisher fixes and
  feature changes therefore depend on a firmware release.

### Published Topics

The native publisher exposes these topics simultaneously. All messages carry the hardware PTP timestamp in `header.stamp`. The `rt` prefix is the DDS-level name: in ROS 2 tools, `rt<namespace>/cloud/all_points` appears as `<namespace>/cloud/all_points`, for example `/cloud/all_points`.

The multiScan200 and picoScan100 publish the same PointCloud2 and LaserScan topics. The multiScan200 also publishes the `ambient_light` and `imu` topics, and a PointCloud2 topic per segment and echo.

**PointCloud2 topics**

<p class="table-caption" markdown>**Published Topics:** PointCloud2 topic, contents ¹⁾, output frequency, and description.</p>

| PointCloud2 topic | Contents ¹⁾ | Output frequency | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `rt<namespace>/cloud/all_points` | x,y,z,i,p | Scan rate | Valid scan points of all segments and all echoes |
| `rt<namespace>/cloud/all_points_echo0` | x,y,z,i,p | Scan rate | Valid scan points of echo 0 |
| `rt<namespace>/cloud/all_points_echo1` | x,y,z,i,p | Scan rate | Valid scan points of echo 1 (only available if multi-echo is configured) |
| `rt<namespace>/cloud/all_points_echo2` | x,y,z,i,p | Scan rate | Valid scan points of echo 2 (only available if multi-echo is configured) |
| `rt<namespace>/cloud/reflector_points` | x,y,z,i,p | Scan rate | Valid scan points that were recognized as reflectors |
| `rt<namespace>/cloud/segment[s]` | x,y,z,i,p | Segment frequency | Valid scan points of a selected segment s (only available for segments that are available after application of the angle range filter) |
| `rt<namespace>/cloud/segment[s]_echo[e]` | x,y,z,i,p | Segment frequency | multiScan200 only: valid scan points of echo e in segment s (only available for segments that are available after application of the angle range filter and depending on the configuration of the echo filter) |

¹⁾ intensity (i): RSSI with value range: 0.0 ... 1.0; properties (p): Bit mask 0b00000001 indicates whether this measurement point was recognized as a reflection. On the multiScan200, `sWN rosPointCloud2Content` selects the optional channels RSSI, properties, time offset, and ring (layer index); see the [multiScan200 CoLa Telegram Listing](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/multiScan200/api-cola-telegrams/#set-optional-channels-of-pointcloud2-topics-swn-rospointcloud2content).

**Additional topics (multiScan200)**

<p class="table-caption" markdown>**Published Topics:** topic and content.</p>

| Topic | Content |
| --- | --- |
| `ambient_light` | Passive ambient light image, synchronized with the point cloud |
| `imu` | IMU data: acceleration, angular velocity, and orientation |

**LaserScan / MultiEchoLaserScan topics**

<p class="table-caption" markdown>**Published Topics:** LaserScan / MultiEchoLaserScan topic, data format, contents ¹⁾, output frequency, and description.</p>

| LaserScan / MultiEchoLaserScan topic | Data format | Contents ¹⁾ | Output frequency | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `rt<namespace>/scan/all_points` | MultiEchoLaserScan | x,y,z,i | Scan rate | Valid scan points of all segments and all echoes |
| `rt<namespace>/scan/all_points_echo0` | LaserScan | x,y,z,i | Scan rate | Valid scan points of echo 0 |
| `rt<namespace>/scan/all_points_echo1` | LaserScan | x,y,z,i | Scan rate | Valid scan points of echo 1 (only available if multi-echo is configured) |
| `rt<namespace>/scan/all_points_echo2` | LaserScan | x,y,z,i | Scan rate | Valid scan points of echo 2 (only available if multi-echo is configured) |
| `rt<namespace>/scan/segment[s]` | MultiEchoLaserScan | x,y,z,i | Segment frequency | Only for available segment s (only available for segments that are available after application of the angle range filter) |
| `rt<namespace>/scan/segment[s]_echo[e]` | LaserScan | x,y,z,i | Segment frequency | Only for available segments and echo e (only available for segments that are available after application of the angle range filter and depending on the configuration of the echo filter) |

¹⁾ intensity (i): Value range 0.0-1.0 for natural targets, 1.05 for detected reflector

### Frame and Position Parameters

Set the frames and the mounting position on the device; Native ROS 2 has no ROS parameters. Use the CoLa telegrams below, the REST endpoint of the same name, or the web interface.

<div class="center-table-headers" markdown="1">

<p class="table-caption" markdown>**Frame and Position Parameters:** parameter, CoLa telegram, and effect.</p>

| Parameter | CoLa telegram | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Frame ID | `sWN rosFrameId` | `header.frame_id` of the published messages |
| Parent frame ID | `sWN rosParentFrameId` | Parent frame of the sensor transform, for example `world` |
| Namespace | `sWN rosNamespace` | Prepended to all topic names; empty for no namespace |
| Sensor position | `sWN SensorPosition` | Mounting position (x, y, z in mm) and orientation (yaw, pitch, roll in 1/10000°), published as a transform on `/tf` |
| Domain ID | `sWN rosDomainId` | ROS 2 domain ID (0-232); must match `ROS_DOMAIN_ID` on the host |

</div>

For the telegram structures and examples, see the CoLa Telegram Listings of the [multiScan200](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/multiScan200/api-cola-telegrams/#measurement-output-telegram) and the [picoScan100](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/picoScan100/api-cola-telegrams/). After changing the static IP address, restart the device so that the topics are published correctly.

### DDS Capabilities

Native ROS 2 uses Cyclone DDS and is tested with the
`rmw_cyclonedds_cpp` ROS middleware (RMW) implementation. Other RMW
implementations can cause incompatibilities, even when they also use DDS.
Use Cyclone DDS for the tested setup; validate interoperability before
using a different middleware.

Because the device runs a DDS participant in its firmware, it joins the ROS 2 network as a first-class peer:

- **Interoperability:** Compatible ROS 2 nodes, MathWorks ROS Toolbox, and custom DDS clients can subscribe directly, subject to middleware compatibility.
- **Multiple subscribers:** The sensor publishes once per scan; adding subscribers does not add another device-side publishing step.
- **Per-subscriber QoS:** Subscribers can negotiate policies independently, such as `BEST_EFFORT` for control and `RELIABLE` for recording.
- **Automatic discovery:** RTPS discovery finds subscribers without a broker or static IP table.
- **Hardware timestamps:** `header.stamp` is set at the hardware scan trigger. With PTP synchronization, it aligns with other sensors.

### Video Tutorials

*How to use native ROS 2 (DDS) on Linux.*
*How to use native ROS 2 (DDS) on Windows.*

## sick_scan_xd

Compatible with: LRS4000 multiScan100 picoScan100

The `sick_scan_xd` driver runs as a ROS 1 or ROS 2 node on the host. It
receives sensor data, assembles complete scans, and publishes ROS messages.
Choose this approach when you need host-side decoding control, IMU data on
ROS topics where supported, or integration with a device that has no native
publisher. It also supports recording and playback with rosbag `.db3` files.
To install it, follow
[Building the driver: ROS 2 on Linux](https://github.com/SICKAG/sick_scan_xd/blob/develop/README.md#ros-2-on-linux)
or [ROS 2 on Windows](https://github.com/SICKAG/sick_scan_xd/blob/develop/README.md#ros-2-on-windows-jazzy-kilted--lyrical)
in the README. Then start the launch file for your device as described in
[Running the driver](https://github.com/SICKAG/sick_scan_xd/blob/develop/README.md#running-the-driver).

## CPU Load Comparison

Measurements across 11 picoScan150 profiles used 15-50 Hz scan rates, 0.05-1.0° angular resolutions, 100 scans per method, and IEEE 1588 PTP synchronization. Single-echo `sensor_msgs/LaserScan` data was used for a direct comparison.

<p class="table-caption" markdown>**CPU Load Comparison:** parameter and value.</p>

| Parameter | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Host | Raspberry Pi 4, ARM Cortex-A72, 4 cores, Ubuntu 22.04 |
| Network | Direct Gigabit Ethernet |
| Latency definition | `Δt = treceive_on_host − header.stamp` |

Average system CPU load was **8.5%** for native ROS 2 and **21.5%** for `sick_scan_xd`, expressed as the percentage of one Raspberry Pi 4 CPU core.

# Building Security Example with LiDAR

> Explore a building-monitoring example with LiDAR field evaluation and a video demonstration of teach-in.

Source: https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/beginner-projects/building-security/

# Building Security Example

Compatible with: LRS4000 picoScan100

Security access gates form a transition between secure and non-secure areas
of an airport. An object-detection check can help identify items left in the
gate area before access is granted.

![Security access gate with a red detection area and an inset showing the mounted LiDAR sensor](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/assets/shared-features/security-door-detection-area.png)
*Example security-door installation. The red overlay illustrates the detection area; the inset shows the LiDAR sensor mounting position.*

A compact 2D LiDAR sensor can monitor a configured detection zone and report
objects that interrupt the scan or differ from a taught reference contour.
This can support a security workflow concerned with prohibited items, such
as weapons, but LiDAR object detection alone does not identify an object's
type or determine whether it is prohibited. Validate detection coverage and
performance for the installation and combine it with the required security
checks.

## Suggested Data Path

Configure the detection zone with [teach-in](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/on-device-applications/field-evaluation/#teach-in):

1. In SOPASair, open the **Object Detection** application and select **Teach-in** in the field configuration.
2. Set the distances in front of and behind the object and the minimum teach-in time, then click **Start**.
3. Keep the gate area empty and stable, stop the teach-in, and save the field evaluation configuration.
4. Check the result: with the gate area empty, the field is free; place a test object in it and confirm that the field is infringed.

## Example Solution

The following video demonstrates teach-in for a building-security example.

*Teach-in demonstration for the building-security example.*

# Bulk Scan with LiDAR: Material Height on a Conveyor

> Measure the height of woodchips or other bulk material on a conveyor belt with on-device perpendicular distance measurement.

Source: https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/beginner-projects/bulk-scan/

# Bulk Scan

Compatible with: LRS4000 picoScan100

This project measures the height of woodchips or other bulk material on a
conveyor belt. Mounted above the belt, the sensor scans the material surface
and reports its distance to the empty belt. It is a height measurement, not a
calibrated volume measurement; a volume estimate needs your own processing.

![LiDAR mounted above a conveyor belt carrying woodchips, with the scan area highlighted in purple](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/assets/shared-features/woodchip-volume-conveyor.png)
*Example woodchip conveyor installation. The highlighted scan area covers the material profile across the belt.*

Use [Perpendicular Distance Measurement](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/on-device-applications/perpendicular-distance-measurement/)
as a starting point for measuring material height:

1. In SOPASair, open **Application > Perpendicular distance measurement** and add an evaluation group.
2. Draw the zone across the belt and set the reference line to the empty belt surface.
3. Save the configuration and read the minimum and maximum distances from the result list or `GET /api/perpendicularDistanceResult`.
4. Check the result: with an empty belt, no distance is reported; with a test object of known height on the belt, the maximum distance matches that height.

To estimate volume throughput, your application can calculate the cross-sectional area from the scan profile and multiply it by the belt speed.

*Perpendicular-distance measurement demonstration for the woodchip example.*

# 3D Height Measurement with LiDAR

> Measure body height with a multiScan100 by evaluating the maximum perpendicular distance above a floor reference inside a 3D field.

Source: https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/beginner-projects/height-measurement/

# 3D Height Measurement

Compatible with: multiScan100

A multiScan100 can measure the body height of a person in a defined area.
The sensor scans the area in 3D, while perpendicular-distance evaluation
measures the detected points relative to the floor. The maximum distance
inside the evaluation field represents the person's height.

![People passing through a LiDAR height-measurement area](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/assets/beginner-projects/height-measurement-application.png)
*A 3D LiDAR measures people as they pass through a defined detection area.*

## Suggested Data Path

1. Mount the multiScan100 so its field of view covers the measuring area and
   the top of the person's head remains within the scan range.
2. Create an evaluation group in **Application > Perpendicular distance
   measurement** and draw a field around the measuring area.
3. Use the floor as the reference plane. Keep walls, door frames, and other
   fixed objects outside the field so they cannot become the maximum value.
4. Configure the object-detection settings for stable measurements.
5. Read the minimum and maximum perpendicular distances from the evaluation
   result. Use the maximum distance as the measured body height.

For configuration and result-access details, see
[Perpendicular Distance Measurement](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/on-device-applications/perpendicular-distance-measurement/).

## Example Solution

The following screenshot shows the evaluation in SOPASair. The 3D field
covers the person above the floor, and the result list reports the minimum
and maximum distances for the evaluation.

![SOPASair perpendicular-distance evaluation with a 3D measuring field around a person and a maximum distance of 1766 mm](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/assets/beginner-projects/height-measurement-perpendicular-distance.png)
*Height-measurement example using perpendicular distance. The maximum distance of 1766 mm represents the measured body height.*

Validate the setup with people of known height and verify that the reported
maximum remains stable as a person moves through the measuring area.

# Reversing Assistant

> Build a picoScan warning aid that finds the nearest obstacle and flashes the sensor LEDs faster as the obstacle gets closer.

Source: https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/beginner-projects/reversing-assistant/

# Reversing Assistant

Compatible with: picoScan100

When reversing a vehicle, objects behind it can be difficult to see and the
available stopping distance decreases quickly. A LiDAR sensor can monitor this
area and provide an immediate warning: the closer the nearest obstacle is, the
faster the sensor LEDs flash.

![Forklift with a LiDAR sensor monitoring the reversing area and detecting a pallet](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/assets/beginner-projects/reverse-camera-application.png)
*The LiDAR monitors the reversing area. A shorter distance to the nearest obstacle produces a faster warning flash.*

## Before You Start

- Connect the picoScan150 and the development computer to the same network.
- Mount the sensor so its field of view covers the monitored reversing area.
- Build and install
  [sick_perception_sdk](https://github.com/SICKAG/sick_perception_sdk) with the
  `picoScan100` examples.
- Change `receiverAddress` if the computer does not use `192.168.0.100`.
- Set the environment variable `SICK_PASSWORD` to the Service password. The default passwords are documented in the operating instructions of your device. Do not pass them on, and change them during commissioning.

## Minimal Example

This example is based on the SDK's UDP streaming example. The point-cloud
callback only calculates the flash period; the main loop performs the REST
writes so scan reception is not blocked by an HTTP request.

The warning uses the radial range supplied by the scanner in the Compact scan
data. Every point in the received frame is considered.

This example is adapted from the
[sick_perception_sdk UDP streaming example](https://github.com/SICKAG/sick_perception_sdk/blob/main/examples/shared/data_streaming_udp.cpp)
and is licensed under the MIT License. The upstream copyright and permission
notice applies to copies or substantial portions of this example:

<details>
<summary>Expand to view the complete C++ example</summary>

```cpp
#include <sick_perception_sdk/compact_format/PointCloud/UnorganizedPointCloud.hpp>
#include <sick_perception_sdk/drivers/picoScan100/PicoScan100Driver.hpp>
#include <sick_perception_sdk/sensor_configuration/HttpClient/httplib_client/HttpClient.hpp>
#include <sick_perception_sdk/sensor_configuration/picoScan150/PicoScan150Configurator.hpp>

#include <atomic>
#include <algorithm>
#include <chrono>
#include <csignal>
#include <cstdint>
#include <cstdlib>
#include <limits>
#include <memory>
#include <thread>

// The signal handler changes this flag when the user presses Ctrl+C.
std::atomic<bool> running {true};

int main()
{
  // Change these addresses if the sensor or computer uses another subnet.
  constexpr char sensorAddress[] = "192.168.0.1";
  sick::IpV4Address receiverAddress {"192.168.0.100"};
  constexpr std::uint16_t scanPort = 2115;

  // Read the Service password from the environment instead of the source code.
  char const* password = std::getenv("SICK_PASSWORD");
  if (password == nullptr)
  {
    return 1;
  }

  auto const httpClient =
    std::make_shared<sick::httplib_client::HttpClient>(sensorAddress, 80);
  sick::picoScan150::v2_3_3::Configurator configurator(
    httpClient, sick::UserLevel::Service, password);

  configurator.enableScanDataStreamingCompactUdp(receiverAddress, scanPort);

  // The scan callback writes these values while the main loop reads them.
  std::atomic<int> flashPeriodMs {0};
  std::atomic<std::chrono::steady_clock::time_point> lastFrame {
    std::chrono::steady_clock::time_point {}};

  // Request the scanner-provided radial range for every point.
  sick::point_cloud::PointCloudConfiguration pointCloudConfig;
  pointCloudConfig.fields.enableSpherical = true;

  sick::picoScan100::Driver driver;
  driver.scanDataReceiver()
    .setup(scanPort)
    .setOnNewFrameCallback(
      [&](sick::point_cloud::UnorganizedPointCloud const& cloud) {
        // Find the closest valid radial range in the complete scan frame.
        float nearest = std::numeric_limits<float>::infinity();
        for (std::size_t i = 0; i < cloud.numberOfPoints(); ++i)
        {
          nearest = std::min(nearest, cloud.getRange(i));
        }

        // Store one full LED on/off period for the selected warning level.
        flashPeriodMs =
          nearest <= 0.5F ? 333 :
          nearest <= 2.0F ? 500 :
          nearest < std::numeric_limits<float>::infinity() ? 2000 : 0;
        lastFrame = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
      },
      pointCloudConfig);
  driver.run();

  std::signal(SIGINT, [](int) { running = false; });
  bool ledOn = false;
  while (running)
  {
    // Treat missing scan data as "no obstacle" after 500 ms.
    bool const scanIsCurrent =
      std::chrono::steady_clock::now() - lastFrame.load() <=
      std::chrono::milliseconds(500);
    int const period = scanIsCurrent ? flashPeriodMs.load() : 0;

    if (period == 0)
    {
      if (ledOn)
      {
        configurator.setLEDEnable(false);
        ledOn = false;
      }
      std::this_thread::sleep_for(std::chrono::milliseconds(50));
      continue;
    }

    // Toggling after half a period produces the requested flash frequency.
    ledOn = !ledOn;
    configurator.setLEDEnable(ledOn);
    std::this_thread::sleep_for(std::chrono::milliseconds(period / 2));
  }

  configurator.setLEDEnable(true);
}
```

</details>

Add the source as another picoScan100 example target and link it with
`sick_perception_sdk::drivers` and
`sick_perception_sdk::sensor_configuration`, like the SDK's
`data_streaming_udp` example. Stop it with **Ctrl+C**; the final call enables
the LEDs again, which is their default state.

## Expected Behavior

If no scan frame arrives for 500 ms, the scan is treated as stale and the LEDs
are switched off.

<p class="table-caption" markdown>**Expected Behavior:** nearest point, flash frequency, and result.</p>

| Nearest point | Flash frequency | Result |
| ---: | ---: | --- |
| No obstacle or stale scan | Off | LEDs stay off |
| 0 m to 0.5 m | 3 Hz | Fast warning |
| More than 0.5 m to 2 m | 2 Hz | Medium warning |
| More than 2 m | 0.5 Hz | Slow warning |

Move a test object through the sensor's field of view and check that the reported behavior
changes monotonically: every smaller distance must produce the same or a
shorter period. Test only in a controlled area; this example is a warning aid,
not a safety function.

## Optional Digital Output

The same `ledOn` value can be sent to `POST /api/SetOutput` at the same cadence.
First configure that output's source as **SOPAS command**, then call the SDK's
`setOutput()` method with the output number and value. Do not use
`OutputState` for this: that endpoint only reads the current output states.

# Native ROS 2 SLAM with picoScan150

> Explore driverless-vehicle localization with LiDAR, with a beginner introduction to ROS 2 and saved-map localization using SLAM Toolbox.

Source: https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/beginner-projects/native-ros2-slam/

# Native ROS 2 SLAM

Compatible with: picoScan100

<div class="tool-intro" markdown>

![ROS 2](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/assets/integration-notes/ros2-logo.png)
Reliable localization is essential for autonomous driving, driverless-vehicle
navigation, and a smooth material flow. High-resolution LiDAR measurements
help map the surroundings. Localization software compares measurements with
the map to estimate the vehicle's position and orientation, also called its
**pose**. Accuracy depends on the environment, sensor setup, and software
configuration.

</div>

![Warehouse scene showing a mobile robot, LiDAR scan lines, occupancy map, and localization status display](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/assets/beginner-projects/slam-localization-example.png)
*Illustration of LiDAR mapping and localization with a mobile robot, occupancy map, and pose estimate.*

## What You'll Learn

- How the native ROS 2 `LaserScan` topic of a picoScan150 feeds SLAM Toolbox.
- The difference between mapping and localization, and why scan-matching
  odometry replaces wheel encoders here.
- How to check the TF tree and the map-relative pose in RViz.

## ROS 2 for Beginners

For the simplest setup, run this example on an Ubuntu system supported by
your ROS 2 distribution. ROS 2, SLAM Toolbox, and RViz are readily available
as packages on supported Ubuntu releases. Match the Ubuntu version to the
ROS 2 distribution's installation requirements.

ROS 2 is a software framework for connecting robot components. It is not a
complete robot application: you combine programs called **nodes** to handle
tasks such as receiving sensor data, estimating position, and driving motors.
Nodes exchange messages over named **topics**.

For this example, a LiDAR integration publishes scan measurements. Mapping
or localization software consumes those measurements together with robot
motion information. Coordinate transforms (**TF**) describe how the sensor,
robot, and map are positioned relative to one another.

## Mapping, Localization, and Navigation

<p class="table-caption" markdown>**Mapping, Localization, and Navigation:** task and what it does.</p>

| Task | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| SLAM | Simultaneous localization and mapping: builds a map while estimating the robot's pose. |
| Localization | Estimates the robot's pose within an existing map. |
| Navigation | Uses the pose and a destination to plan and follow a route while considering obstacles. |

This example only builds a map and estimates the vehicle's pose within it.
Use **SLAM Toolbox** for both stages: first run mapping, then load the saved
pose graph in localization mode. A navigation stack, route planner, and
motion controller are not required for this example.

## Suggested Data Path

The typical data path is:

**LiDAR LaserScan → scan-matching odometry + TF → SLAM Toolbox → map-relative pose in RViz**

This example uses LiDAR scan matching to estimate movement, without wheel
encoders. Run a separate scan-matching odometry node alongside SLAM Toolbox;
excluding encoders does not remove SLAM Toolbox's odometry requirement.
Provide a suitable `LaserScan` topic to both nodes.

## Example Solution

*LiDAR mapping and localization example with ROS 2 and SLAM Toolbox.*

## Check the Result

- `ros2 topic list` shows the scan topic of the sensor.
- In RViz, the map grows while you move the sensor slowly, and walls stay sharp
  instead of doubling.
- In localization mode with the saved pose graph, the pose follows the sensor
  and the map does not shift.

## Project Prompt

# picoScan150 Jump & Run: IMU-Controlled Browser Game

> Turn a picoScan into a game controller: decode the IMU stream with a Kaitai Python parser and steer a browser jump-and-run game by moving the sensor.

Source: https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/beginner-projects/imu-jump-and-run/

# picoScan150 Jump & Run

Compatible with: picoScan100

Build **picoScan150 Jump & Run** and use the built-in IMU of a picoScan as a game controller. Move the sensor left
or right and the player runs with it; a quick upward hop makes it jump. Points
grow with time, and the game gets faster every 15 seconds. No scan data is
used.

*picoScan150 Jump &amp; Run: moving the sensor steers the player.*

## What You'll Learn

- How to enable the IMU stream over REST and receive it as Compact type 2 over UDP.
- How to check the CRC32 and decode the telegrams with a generated Kaitai parser.
- How to turn acceleration into robust movement events.

## Before You Start

- A picoScan with IMU streaming, for example picoScan150, on the same network
  as your computer ([Getting Started](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/getting-started/)).
- Python, a browser, the
  [Kaitai Struct compiler and runtime](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/integration-notes/kaitai-struct-parsers/#generate-from-the-command-line),
  and [sick_scan_rest_client](https://github.com/SICKAG/sick_scan_rest_client).
- Hold the sensor firmly with slack in the cables. Short moves of 10 to 20 cm
  are enough.
- Set the environment variable `SICK_PASSWORD` to the Service password. The
  default passwords are documented in the operating instructions of your
  device. Do not pass them on, and change them during commissioning.

## Data Path

**picoScan IMU → UDP → CRC32 check → Kaitai Python parser → motion
controller → local web server → browser game**

Python receives the UDP datagrams and serves the Canvas game on `127.0.0.1`.
Generate the parser from the official
[Compact frame](https://github.com/SICKAG/KaitaiStructDescriptions/blob/public/formats/compact_frame.ksy)
and [type-2 IMU](https://github.com/SICKAG/KaitaiStructDescriptions/blob/public/formats/type_2_imu.ksy)
definitions. The parser does not verify the checksum; check the CRC32 first
([Reception and Validation](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/integration-notes/kaitai-struct-parsers/#reception-and-validation)).

## Configure IMU Output

The game sets up the stream through the
[REST interface](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/configuration/rest-interface/) at start and disables it
on exit:

```python
import os

from sick_scan_rest_client.client import RESTClient

client = RESTClient("192.168.0.1")  # sensor IP address
client.setUserLevel("Service", os.environ["SICK_PASSWORD"])
client.writeVariable("ImuDataEthSettings",
                     {"Protocol": 1, "IPAddress": [192, 168, 0, 100], "Port": 7503})
client.writeVariable("ImuDataEnable", True)
```

*Send the IMU stream by UDP (<code>Protocol</code> 1) to the computer at 192.168.0.100, port 7503. The change is RAM-only.*

Keep both IP addresses and the port configurable. If the sensor streams but
nothing arrives, the computer's firewall is the usual cause; allow the port or
pick one that is permitted.

## How Movement Works

The game uses gravity-corrected acceleration, not tilt. To calibrate, hold the sensor
still, then push it right once.

<div class="imu-movement" role="group" aria-label="Move the picoScan left or right to steer, or lift it in a quick hop to jump">
  <span class="imu-movement__jump">↑ Quick hop to jump</span>
  <span class="imu-movement__left">← Move left</span>
  <img src="https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/assets/picoScan100/img/product-photo.png" alt="SICK picoScan sensor">
  *Move the sensor sideways to steer; lift it for a quick hop to jump.*
  <span class="imu-movement__right">Move right →</span>
</div>

<p class="table-caption">Game controls.</p>

| Control                   | Response                                    |
| ------------------------- | ------------------------------------------- |
| Move sensor left or right | Player runs left or right.                  |
| Quick upward hop          | One jump.                                   |
| Start, Pause, Stop        | Run, freeze, or end the game.               |
| Calibrate                 | Hold still, then push right once.           |
| Settings                  | Sensor IP, computer IP, port, sensitivity.  |
| Arrow keys and Space      | Play without a sensor.                      |

Jump over blocks, dodge falling rocks from level 2, and collect coins. You
score 10 points per second and 50 per coin. The game pauses if IMU data stops
for 500 ms.

## Check the Result

- Without a sensor, play with the keyboard; the high score survives a
  restart.
- With the sensor, the status shows about 100 valid packets per second.
- Holding still or tilting slowly does not move the player; a short move
  right does, then stops.
- A quick hop gives exactly one jump; a sideways push gives none.
- Quitting the program switches the IMU stream off.

## Project Prompt

Paste this prompt into your coding assistant in a new workspace. It asks for
the receiver, the game, tests, and a Windows executable.

<details>
<summary>Expand to view the complete project prompt</summary>

```text
Build a beginner-friendly level-two project called "picoScan150 Jump & Run":
a SICK picoScan150 IMU is the game controller for a basic browser
jump-and-run game. The player moves left and
right when I move the sensor left and right (use the measured acceleration,
not tilt), and jumps when I lift the sensor with a quick upward hop.
Deliver working files, not a plan. Work in a new folder outside the
developer guide. Use Python 3.12, the Kaitai Struct Python runtime, requests,
sick_scan_rest_client (https://github.com/SICKAG/sick_scan_rest_client) and
plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript with Canvas. Use only the Python standard
library for the web server. No ROS, SICK SDK, scan data, point clouds,
frontend framework or external game assets. Keep the code easy to follow.
Draw the player as a small picoScan: grey housing with a blue SICK badge,
black optics dome with a moving red scan point, short legs, and a faint scan
fan in the running direction.

1. Configuration
Read config.json next to the program (create it with defaults on first start)
and allow command-line overrides: sensor IP (default 192.168.0.1), PC IP on
the sensor network (default 192.168.0.100), UDP port (default 7503), local
HTTP port (default 8765), --no-configure and --no-browser. Validate IPv4
addresses and ports. Offer the same settings in a Settings dialog in the game,
list the PC's local IPv4 addresses as suggestions, save changes back to
config.json and reconnect without restarting the program.

2. Sensor setup with REST
At start, in a background thread, use sick_scan_rest_client: RESTClient(ip),
setUserLevel("Service", password from config), then writeVariable
"ImuDataEthSettings" = {"Protocol": 1, "IPAddress": [PC IP octets],
"Port": udp port} and "ImuDataEnable" = true. Check reachability with a short
TCP connect to port 80 first, because the client sets no timeouts. Bypass any
system HTTP proxy for the sensor IP. writeVariable returns (ok, data);
check ok. Both variables need the Service level. Use UDP: TCP output
(Protocol 2) was refused in tests, and polling the IMU over REST only
updates at about 4 Hz, which is too slow for a game. These are RAM-only
changes; do not call WriteEeprom. Show the result in the UI. On exit set
ImuDataEnable = false. On Windows, atexit does not run when the console
window is closed, so also register a console control handler
(SetConsoleCtrlHandler) for close and Ctrl+Break. Keep scan settings
untouched.

3. Receive and decode with the real Kaitai parser
Generate Python from SICKAG/KaitaiStructDescriptions (public branch),
formats/compact_frame.ksy with all imported formats, using
kaitai-struct-compiler -t python --outdir <dir> formats/*.ksy. Keep the
generated modules unmodified and record the command. They import each other
as top-level modules, so add their folder to sys.path, and use the
kaitaistruct runtime 0.11 or newer. Do not replace Kaitai
with a hand-written struct parser. Bind a UDP socket to the PC IP and port,
accept datagrams only from the sensor IP, check the start bytes 02 02 02 02,
verify CRC32 (zlib.crc32 over all bytes except the trailing 4-byte
little-endian checksum), then parse with CompactFrame and accept only
telegram_type == 2. Count good and rejected frames, compute the packet rate
(about 100 Hz on picoScan150) and keep the receiver alive on bad packets.
Report bind errors clearly (for example, the PC IP is not on this computer).
Record a few hundred real frames to a file for the tests.

4. Turn acceleration into controls
Rotate the acceleration into the world frame with the orientation quaternion
(w, x, y, z) and subtract a gravity/bias vector, so tilting the sensor does
not look like sideways motion. On picoScan150 the quaternion is
gravity-referenced: R(q) * acc is about (0, 0, 9.8) at rest. Without the
rotation, a 20 degree tilt leaks about 3.4 m/s^2 into the sideways axis and
the velocity drifts. Yaw has no magnetometer reference and can drift slowly,
so offer recalibration. Estimate that vector automatically from the
first 1.5 s, and track it slowly while the sensor is quiet.
Calibrate button: 1.5 s still (reject if the per-axis standard deviation is
above 0.35 m/s^2), then "move the sensor quickly to the RIGHT once": the
horizontal direction of the strongest push sample (above 2 m/s^2) becomes
the right axis. Without calibration, use the sensor y axis projected into
the horizontal plane. Add an invert option.
Sideways input: dead zone 0.35 m/s^2, then integrate into a velocity with a
leak (time constant 0.8 s while moving, 0.12 s after 0.15 s of quiet), so it
returns to zero when the sensor stops. The leak recovers only about half
of the real movement, so scale the velocity in the game (about 2600 px per
m/s at sensitivity 1). Do not double-integrate to an absolute position; it
drifts within seconds. Jump: vertical linear acceleration
above 3.5 m/s^2, re-arm below 1.0 m/s^2, cooldown 0.6 s; count jumps with a
sequence number so the browser consumes each jump once. Use sensor
timestamps for dt.

5. Game
Serve the game on 127.0.0.1 only. Push velocity, accelerations, jump
counter, calibration state, packet statistics and sensor status to the
browser with Server-Sent Events at about 50 Hz. Accept POST requests only
with Content-Type application/json. Give each calibration request an id and
let the dialog react only to status messages with that id, so a stale
"ready" message does not close it early. If the HTTP port is busy, try the
next ones and open the browser on the port actually used.
Canvas 960x540, scaled to the window without horizontal scrolling. The world
scrolls left; the player moves with sensor velocity times a sensitivity
setting, clamped to the screen; arrow keys and Space also work. Ground blocks
to jump over, from level 2 falling rocks with a shadow warning to dodge
sideways, coins for +50. Score 10 points per second of active play, level up
every 15 s with faster scrolling and more obstacles, capped so jumps stay
possible. Collision ends the run.
Buttons: Start, Pause/Resume, Stop, Calibrate, Settings. Show score, level,
high score (saved in highscore.json next to the program), sensor status with
packet rate, a sideways acceleration and velocity meter, and a jump light.
If data is older than 500 ms while playing in sensor mode, pause and require
Resume. If no packets arrive 3 s after a successful configuration, show a
hint to check the PC IP and the firewall, or choose another UDP port.
Corporate Windows firewalls often block inbound UDP and ignore local rules,
or allow it only while the Ethernet network is classified as Private; then
use a port the policy allows (for example 30719 in our tests).

6. Tests and delivery
Unit-test the receiver with recorded real frames (good CRC, corrupted byte,
wrong start bytes) and the controller with synthetic samples: still sensor,
noise below the dead zone, push right/left, calibration learning a different
axis, invert, a tilted sensor that must not drift, a push while tilted,
an upward hop giving one jump, a sideways push giving no jump, and a shaky
calibration being rejected. Provide a PowerShell build script that runs the
tests and builds one console .exe with PyInstaller (--onefile, add the static
folder as data, pass the Kaitai folder with --paths and the generated modules
as hidden imports, name it picoScan150JumpAndRun). Include a README
with run, settings, calibration and firewall notes. Test with the real sensor
and state clearly what was verified with hardware.
```

</details>

# Smart Shelf with picoScan

> Detect which shelf compartment a hand reaches into. Use on-sensor perpendicular distance, WebSocket events and a browser shelf with pick-to-light checks.

Source: https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/beginner-projects/smart-shelf/

# Smart Shelf

Compatible with: picoScan100

Smart shelves record which compartment goods are taken from or put into. A 2D
LiDAR scans a light curtain in front of the rack. The sensor evaluates the
data itself and reports where the curtain is crossed. Software turns this
position into a compartment and checks if the pick was correct.

![Shelf with a LiDAR light curtain in front of the compartments](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/assets/beginner-projects/smart-shelf-application.png)

*Smart shelf: the scan plane in front of the rack shows where a hand reaches in.*

In this project, a picoScan stands in front of a desktop monitor. The browser
draws a shelf on the screen. Touch a compartment with a pen and it lights up.

## What You'll Learn

- How on-device perpendicular distance turns the scan plane into a light curtain.
- How a browser receives sensor events directly over WebSocket.
- How a three-point teach-in maps sensor coordinates to screen positions.

## Before You Start

- A picoScan, for example picoScan150, on the same network as your computer
  ([Getting Started](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/getting-started/)).
- A browser. No server, Python or SICK SDK is needed.
- Place the picoScan on the desk at the lower-left edge of the monitor so the
  scan plane runs just in front of the screen.

## Solution Path

**Perpendicular distance on the sensor → WebSocket event → pen position →
compartment → dwell time → pick check**

1. Set up [Perpendicular Distance Measurement](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/on-device-applications/perpendicular-distance-measurement/)
   with a field that covers the screen. Use a small minimum object size, for
   example 10 mm, so a pen is detected.
2. The browser subscribes to `perpendicularDistanceResult` on
   `ws://192.168.0.1/apievents` ([WebSocket Events](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/data-streaming/websocket-events/)).
3. The middle of the minimum and maximum distance positions is the pen
   position in millimeters.
4. A three-point teach-in maps sensor millimeters to screen pixels.
5. The pen must stay in one compartment for 150 ms to count as a pick.

![Sketch of the picoScan on the desk at the lower-left edge of the monitor, scanning just in front of the screen](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/assets/beginner-projects/smart-shelf-setup.svg)

*Setup: the picoScan stands at the lower-left screen edge and scans just in front of the screen. The laser beam measures in polar coordinates; the sensor reports the perpendicular distance d to a horizontal reference line.*

![SOPASair perpendicular distance field in front of the monitor](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/assets/beginner-projects/smart-shelf-perpendicular-distance.png)

*Perpendicular distance field in SOPASair. The field covers the screen in front of the sensor.*

The browser connects to the sensor directly. It registers once and then gets
an event each time the result changes:

```json
{"type": "register", "event": "perpendicularDistanceResult", "clientId": 1}
```

*Register message for the perpendicular distance result.*

Each event carries one entry per evaluation. Distances and positions are in
millimeters:

```json
{
  "type": "event",
  "event": "perpendicularDistanceResult",
  "clientId": 1,
  "status": 0,
  "data": {
    "perpendicularDistanceResult": {
      "timestamp": 4773260000,
      "evaluations": [
        {
          "evaluationId": 1,
          "minimumDistance": 176,
          "maximumDistance": 184,
          "minimumDistancePosition": {"x": 318, "y": -176, "z": 0},
          "maximumDistancePosition": {"x": 322, "y": -184, "z": 0}
        }
      ]
    }
  }
}
```

*Example event with a pen in the field. The pen position is the middle of both positions: x 320 mm, y −180 mm.*

- `minimumDistance` and `maximumDistance` are the smallest and largest
  perpendicular distances to the reference line inside the field.
- `minimumDistancePosition` and `maximumDistancePosition` are the scan points
  with these distances, in sensor coordinates.
- The register reply has the same `data` and already holds the current
  result.

An empty field reports all distances and positions as zero. The app treats
this as "no object".

![Browser shelf with pick-to-light target and live pen position](https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/assets/beginner-projects/smart-shelf-browser.png)

*Smart shelf in the browser: the blue compartment is the pick target, the yellow dot is the pen.*

## Check the Result

- Without a sensor, a mouse drag over a compartment lights it up.
- With the sensor, the status shows "Connected" and the pen position
  updates when you touch the screen.
- After the teach-in, the yellow dot sits under the pen tip.
- A quick pass through a compartment does not count; holding the pen in
  one does.
- In pick-to-light mode, the target flashes green and other compartments
  flash red.

## Project Prompt

Paste this prompt into your coding assistant in a new workspace. It asks for
the browser app, tests and a README.

<details>
<summary>Expand to view the complete project prompt</summary>

```text
Build a beginner-friendly level-two project called "picoScan Smart Shelf".
A SICK picoScan100 stands at the lower edge of my desktop monitor. Its
perpendicular distance evaluation is already configured on the sensor and
covers the screen. The browser draws a shelf on the screen. When I touch a
compartment with a pen, the compartment lights up.
Deliver working files, not a plan. Work in a new folder outside the
developer guide. Use plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript with Canvas. No build
step, framework, server, Python or SICK SDK. Opening index.html must be
enough. Keep the code easy to follow.

Sensor data:
- Connect the browser directly to ws://<sensor-ip>/apievents. Default IP
  192.168.0.1. WebSockets need no CORS, so this works from file://.
- Send {"type":"register","event":"perpendicularDistanceResult",
  "clientId":1}. The register reply already contains the current result;
  handle it like an event. Reconnect after 2 s when the socket closes.
- Events only arrive when the result changes. Run dwell timing on a timer
  or animation frame, not only on incoming messages.
- Read data.perpendicularDistanceResult.evaluations and pick the entry with
  the configured evaluationId (default 1). Use the middle of
  minimumDistancePosition and maximumDistancePosition (x, y in mm) as the
  pen position. If both positions are 0,0, the field is empty.
- Do not call the REST API from the browser. It sends no CORS headers.

Shelf:
- Draw a shelf with uprights, boards and labeled bins (A1, A2 ... with row A
  at the top). Default 3 rows x 4 columns, filling the canvas.
- Default mapping: the field rectangle x -100..600 mm, y -400..0 mm fills
  the canvas; screen up is negative y.
- Add a teach-in: show three crosshair targets near the top-left,
  top-right and bottom-left corners. I hold the pen on each target. Accept
  a point when it stays within 15 mm for 700 ms and average the samples.
  I must lift the pen before the next target. Esc cancels. Solve an affine
  transform from the three points so any rotation or mirroring works.
  After teach-in, ignore sensor input until the pen is lifted.
- A pick is one visit to a compartment that lasts at least the dwell time
  (default 150 ms). A quick pass through a compartment is not a pick.
- Show the live pen as a yellow dot and outline its compartment. Count
  picks per compartment.
- Toolbar: connection status, pen position and compartment, score, and
  buttons for start picking, teach corners, settings and full screen.
- Settings dialog: sensor IP, evaluation ID, rows, columns, dwell time and
  the field rectangle. Store settings and the teach-in in localStorage.
  Warn if the window size changed since the teach-in.

Put parsing, the affine transform, the compartment lookup and the pick
detector in one pure module and test it with node:test. Include a README
with setup, teach-in and test commands. If you add a Python test client,
disable WebSocket keepalive pings; the sensor does not answer them. Test
with the real sensor and state clearly what was verified with hardware.
```

</details>
